data.title: Cult London cinema beloved by Tarantino saved from closure
data.description:
One of the country’s best-loved cinemas has been saved from closure after signing a new lease that will keep its projectors rolling for at least a quarter of a century.

The future of the Prince Charles Cinema in Leicester Square was plunged into doubt almost two years ago amid a bitter dispute with its landlord that prompted an outcry from film fans.

But it has now signed a 25-year lease with Zedwell LSQ, which is ultimately controlled by Asif Aziz, a millionaire property developer, to guarantee the site’s future.

Ben Freedman, the owner of the Prince Charles Cinema, said: “We are delighted to have reached an agreement with Criterion, which secures our long-term future at Leicester Place for the next 25 years.

“Our cinema means an enormous amount to our team, our audiences and the wider arts community. Having this security gives us the confidence to invest in the cinema’s future and continue providing a home for film lovers.

“We are pleased to have reached an agreement that works for both parties and, most importantly, allows us to look forward with real confidence and excitement to the next chapter of the Prince Charles Cinema.”

The Prince Charles, which is the last independent cinema operating in the West End, has won over legions of fans for its offbeat programme of classic and cult films.

The cinema attracts more than 250,000 customers to 850 films and events each year, including all-nighters dedicated to the Jurassic Park and Studio Ghibli films and festive singalongs to favourites such as The Muppet Christmas Carol.

It also shows 70mm pressings of classic films and rarely screened foreign language movies and has attracted praise from Oscar-winning directors, including Paul Thomas Anderson and Quentin Tarantino, who described it as “Mecca for lovers of quality films”.

But the Prince Charles was put at risk of closure early last year by Zedwell, which is part of Mr Aziz’s controversial Criterion Capital, which owns prime property in London’s Leicester Square and Piccadilly Circus.

The cinema accused its landlord of “intimidation” and said it was demanding a rent increase significantly above market rates.

It said Zedwell had also demanded the insertion of a break clause that would require the cinema to vacate the premises at six months’ notice should the company receive planning permission to redevelop the site.

The cinema launched legal proceedings, saying it viewed this as a “clear intention” that its landlord planned to redevelop the building.

The threat prompted an outcry from fans and a petition to save the cinema has gained almost 170,000 signatures.

Westminster council listed the Prince Charles as an asset of community value last year also, giving residents the opportunity to buy the building should it be put up for sale.

The Prince Charles first opened as a theatre in 1962 before gaining a less salubrious reputation in the 1970s as a pornographic film house.

In 1991, the cinema was taken over by Robins Cinemas and began a new life as a repertory cinema playing cult classics for £1 a ticket.

The row is the latest controversy to embroil Criterion, whose flagship project is the London Trocadero, which has been partly converted into the Zedwell, a hotel with more than 700 windowless rooms.

The developer previously came under fire for plans to convert part of the building’s basement into a mosque, while it snapped up the world’s first YMCA on Tottenham Court Road after a legal attempt to save the site failed.

Vaqas Farooq, the chief executive of Criterion Capital, said: “The Prince Charles Cinema is a unique and much-loved part of the West End, and we are delighted to have agreed terms which secure its future at Leicester Place.

“The West End is successful because of its extraordinary blend of culture, entertainment, hospitality and independent enterprise.

“The Prince Charles Cinema is the embodiment of that spirit, and through this agreement, Criterion is delighted to continue supporting a vibrant and diverse West End.”

data.title: The sun will no longer dictate the length of a day
data.description:
A day on Earth is no longer linked to the rising and setting of the sun, after the world’s timekeepers voted to get rid of the leap second.

Since the 1970s, leap seconds have been added to global clocks 27 times, to keep atomic time in sync with Earth’s daily rotation, which has slowed over billions of years.

On such occasions, clocks would pause for a second at 11:59:59 on New Year’s Eve to allow the Earth’s rotation to catch up with atomic time – which is set by the steady tick of electrons rather than planetary movement. The last one happened in 2016.

But on Thursday afternoon, the General Conference on Weights and Measures in Paris approved a resolution to allow the difference between civil time (what people set their clocks to) and solar time to increase from one second to one hour.

It means there will be no more adjustments to clocks until the difference between a solar day and a 24-hour Earth atomic day has slipped by 60 minutes – hundreds of years from now.

‘This is a historical moment’

Noel Dimarcq, a metrologist at the Côte d’Azur Observatory in Nice, France, who formally introduced the resolution, said: “This is a historical moment, a decisive step for UTC [coordinated universal time, an atomic clock equivalent of the solar-based Greenwich Mean Time]. We now have an international reference time scale continuous for the next millennia.”

Keeping atomic clocks in line with solar time was previously deemed important because if it were not corrected it would eventually result in clocks showing the middle of the day occurring at night – although it would take thousands of years for such a difference to become apparent.

A drift of about 25 minutes happens every 500 years.

However, experts say the change is needed because leap seconds have been causing software problems. Earth has been speeding up since 2020, raising the prospect that a negative leap second could soon be needed, making the situation more confusing.

Earth’s time will now run on a new system, called “continuous UTC”, which will come into effect on May 20, 2027 – although it has effectively started already.

Graham Jones, an astrophysicist at the Time and Date website, said: “This has been a long time coming. In the end, the threat of a negative leap second really helped to focus everyone’s minds: in a way, it’s great to see the world come together and take a bold decision.

“And we’re not completely losing our link to solar time. There’s still a limit to how far civil time and solar time can drift apart – we haven’t given ourselves over to atomic time completely.”

Typically, leap seconds were added every two or three years. BT’s speaking clock would add a second’s pause before its third pip while Radio 4 added an extra pip to its 1am bulletin.

In some years, Earth ran bang on time and no adjustment was needed at all.

‘Always errors’ with leap seconds

There have been consequences of tinkering with time. Because leap seconds are only introduced sporadically, it was difficult to implement them in computer code and mistakes could cause systems to fail temporarily.

When a leap second was added in 2012, Mozilla, Reddit, Foursquare, Yelp, LinkedIn and StumbleUpon all reported crashes, and there were problems with the Linux operating system and programs written in Java.

Many computing systems use the network time protocol to keep themselves in sync with the world’s atomic clocks, but most are not programmed to deal with an unexpected extra second.

Google developed a special technique to deal with what it refers to as a “leap smear” and gradually adds milliseconds to its system clocks before the official arrival of the leap second.

Dr Christian Bizouard, at the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service, told Time and Date: “When we apply leap seconds, there are always errors.

“When the leap second system was invented, society did not work with very, very small time resolution. But now there are many applications that need time resolution below one second, for example, financial systems. For that reason, changing UTC by one second is a problem.”

Britain originally argued against abandoning the leap second, fearing that once the link with solar time was broken, it could never be restored, because adding a leap minute or hour to global time would be virtually impossible.

However, on Thursday all 69 member states of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures voted for the change.

data.title: GSK plots £400m Cambridge research hub in push for cancer breakthrough
data.description:
GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) will invest £400m in a major new science hub in Cambridge as part of plans to pour more money into developing new cancer drugs.

The pharmaceuticals giant said it planned to acquire a new 300,000 sq ft site on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, which will house most of its research and development (R&D).

The new centre of excellence will employ more than 1,000 scientists, GSK said, with its researchers developing new vaccines, HIV treatments and cancer drugs.

However, the move will also end the FTSE 100 company’s 50-year relationship with Stevenage, Hertfordshire, which was previously its main UK research base. Some Stevenage staff will be asked to relocate to another lab in nearby Ware.

The investment in Cambridge comes as GSK seeks to ramp up its pipeline of medicines under Luke Miels, its new chief executive, who took on the role from Dame Emma Walmsley at the start of the year.

The company has been accelerating investment in cancer drugs after it acquired US-based Nuvalent in June for nearly £8bn.

GSK won approval from US medical regulators last week for Jideytro, a lung cancer treatment secured as part of the takeover of Nuvalent.

The decision to open a new Cambridge campus will bolster the Government’s efforts to turn the 100-mile corridor between Oxford and Cambridge into an economic powerhouse.

GSK said the investment would build its presence “in the heart of the UK’s life sciences ‘Golden Triangle’” – made up of Oxford, Cambridge and London.

Earlier this year, Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, set out Labour’s ambition to turn the area into a hub for science businesses, building new homes and transport links to create Europe’s “Silicon Valley”.

The Cambridge Biomedical Campus already employs more than 22,000 people and hosts treatments for one million patients each year. GSK hopes to build its links with research hospitals in Cambridge and benefit from proximity to the University of Cambridge.

Mr Miels said: “This investment will accelerate our R&D and help us deliver new, competitive products.”

On Tuesday, GSK also announced plans for a major cost-cutting drive aimed at saving £1.9bn by 2029 to fund the development of new drugs. The savings are expected to include job cuts around the world, including reducing some back-office roles.

Alongside the plans for a new Cambridge site, GSK said it had launched 20 phase three trials as part of its plans to expand its pipeline of treatments.

These trials are the final stage of clinical testing before a drug is submitted to the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency for approval.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, said the £400m investment was “a vote of confidence in British business”.

Life science is one of eight sectors that form part of the Government’s modern industrial strategy.

The investment from GSK comes after its rival AstraZeneca announced that it would pour £200m into its Cambridge site, along with £100m for a project in Macclesfield, Cheshire.

GSK’s relocation to the Cambridge Biomedical Campus means Britain’s two largest pharmaceutical companies will neighbour each other in the city. GSK said it would keep its global headquarters in London.

data.title: Aldi sales growth slows to lowest in two years
data.description:
Aldi’s sales growth has slumped to its lowest level in more than two years as a supermarket price war hits its expansion across Britain.

Sales at the German discounter grew by just 0.4pc compared with the same time last year, below the broader market’s average growth rate of 1pc, according to figures from industry analysts Worldpanel.

That is Aldi’s joint-lowest sales growth since July 2024 as rivals pour money into loyalty card deals and promotions to take on the discounter.

The grocer’s market share also slipped to 10.5pc in the 12 weeks to Oct 4, down from 10.6pc in the same period last year and falling from around 11pc in May 2025.

Its current growth rate of 0.4pc is sharply down from its rapid expansion in the wake of the pandemic, when sales grew nearly 20pc in some months.

While the German chain remains Britain’s fourth-largest supermarket, its expansion is increasingly lagging behind rival discounter Lidl, which reported a 7.1pc increase in sales.

Lidl captured 8.6pc market share, according to Worldpanel’s figures, up from 8.2pc in the same period last year. It climbed above Morrisons to become the UK’s fifth-largest supermarket earlier this year.

Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital, said Aldi was “now the laggard in the sales momentum league”.

He said: “Clearly being crowned Britain’s cheapest supermarket by some third parties does not seem to cut the mustard with shoppers.”

Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons have all been forced to fight back against the growth of European budget grocers by leaning into promotions and members-only pricing.

Of the major supermarkets, only Asda’s sales dipped, down 0.5pc, according to Worldpanel.

Supermarkets poured an additional £250m into promotional deals during the four-week period compared with last year in an effort to take on Aldi’s core low-pricing strategy.

Giles Hurley, the chief executive of Aldi UK and Ireland, criticised competitor loyalty schemes in August, claiming they gave shoppers a “false sense of value”.

Aldi unveiled plans for a fresh assault on rival grocers last month, spending £900m on an expansion drive with plans to open 40 new stores in 2027.

Having first launched in Britain in 1990, Aldi now has more than 1,000 branches across the country.

An Aldi spokesman said: “Our relentless focus on simple, everyday low prices is helping to shield customers from inflationary pressures.

“While this investment can affect short-term value sales, it is attracting more shoppers and driving volume growth ahead of the wider grocery market.”

The Worldpanel data also showed grocery price inflation across Britain rose to 2.5pc in the four weeks to Oct 4, compared with 2.3pc in the four weeks prior.

Fraser McKevitt, the head of retail at Worldpanel, said: “With the Autumn Budget fast approaching, the cost of living continues to weigh heavily on the minds of shoppers.

“And the cost of filling up a car is only adding to the pressure on household budgets.”

data.title: Poland’s central bank crisis exposes European hypocrisy
data.description:
Independent central bankers are becoming an increasing inconvenience for heavily indebted Western governments.

With public borrowing mounting and little political appetite for spending cuts, the temptation to pressure monetary authorities into keeping interest rates low, or otherwise making government debt easier to finance, is growing.

Until now, the resulting confrontations have followed a familiar pattern: populist politicians challenging central bankers who insist on operating independently of the political cycle.

Liz Truss has blamed the Bank of England for helping to bring down her premiership, while Donald Trump’s attacks on Jerome Powell because of interest rates have prompted widespread concern about political interference in the Federal Reserve.

But now, events in Poland are threatening to turn that narrative on its head in a way that could potentially destabilise the region, if not the wider eurozone.

This is because in Warsaw, it is the ostensibly more institutionally minded, pro-European administration of Donald Tusk that is pursuing a central banker associated with the nationalist Right.

And it is the European Central Bank (ECB), having defended the principle of monetary independence against political pressure elsewhere, that may soon find itself having to decide how far that principle extends when the politics are reversed.

The timing is particularly awkward. With France’s fiscal and political difficulties already raising questions about the euro’s resilience, the last thing Frankfurt needs is a confrontation that casts doubt on the consistency of the rules underpinning European monetary governance.

Yet that is precisely the risk emerging from Warsaw.

Last Friday, a Polish parliamentary committee voted to recommend that Adam Glapiński, the governor of the National Bank of Poland, face the state tribunal because of alleged misconduct. The matter now moves to the full parliament, where a vote could take place in early November.

Glapiński is accused of improperly financing government spending through bond purchases during the pandemic, misleading the finance ministry about the bank’s profits and politicising the institution.

He rejects the allegations, arguing that his actions during the pandemic were consistent with the emergency measures adopted by central banks across the developed world.

Indeed, large-scale purchases of government bonds were a central feature of the monetary response to Covid, including at the Bank of England and the ECB. This raises an important question about where the boundary lies between legitimate scrutiny of a central bank governor and the retrospective politicisation of monetary decisions that were widely accepted elsewhere.

Nonetheless, it is true that central bank independence does not confer immunity from the law. The difficulty is that Poland’s institutions are themselves divided about the legal procedures by which a governor can be held accountable.

Since coming to power in 2023, Tusk’s coalition has sought to reverse judicial and institutional reforms introduced by the previous Right-wing Law and Justice government, known as PiS.

Tusk’s supporters – and the EU at large – regard those reforms as an assault on the rule of law. PiS, however, argues that they were necessary to address entrenched political influence within the judiciary, stemming back to the communist era.

The dispute has left Poland with competing interpretations of constitutional authority.

That matters because the contested constitutional tribunal ruled in 2024 that referring the central bank governor to the state tribunal requires a three fifths parliamentary majority, rather than the ordinary absolute majority. It also rejected the provision under which such a referral would automatically suspend him.

The government disputes the validity of those rulings.

In practical terms, the difference could determine whether Glapiński remains in office. If parliament proceeds under the lower threshold, he could maintain that any resulting suspension is unconstitutional, while the government insists it is lawful.

The consequence could be competing claims about who is legally entitled to lead Poland’s central bank.

Complicating matters further is the expiry of the bank’s remaining deputy governor’s term on Nov 4. Without fresh appointments, its management board could fall below the minimum membership required by law to implement monetary policy, just as the dispute surrounding Glapiński approaches its decisive stage.

The same day, the bank is scheduled to announce its next interest rate decision.

Polish policymakers have argued that monetary policy can continue without Glapiński. They may be right. But setting interest rates is only one part of central banking. Implementing decisions, authorising transactions and managing financial assets also require legally recognised authority.

If the zloty came under pressure, for example, and the bank needed to intervene in currency markets, foreign counterparties might reasonably ask whose instructions they were legally entitled to follow.

This could, theoretically, split the bank into rival authorities.

The issue is not entirely without precedent. During Venezuela’s political crisis, rival claims to governmental legitimacy became entangled in litigation concerning access to gold held at the Bank of England.

Poland is obviously a very different case, even though it does also hold a significant amount of gold with the Bank. But the underlying principle is the same: a central bank’s ability to control its reserves depends partly on whether other institutions recognise the authority of those acting on its behalf.

This is where the ECB’s predicament becomes especially interesting.

Although Poland has retained the zloty, its central bank belongs to the European system of central banks. European law provides protections against the arbitrary dismissal of central bank governors and the ECB has previously expressed concern about the proceedings against Glapiński.

Should his suspension become contested, Frankfurt may therefore be required to take a position.

Defending him could bring the ECB into conflict with a Polish government whose efforts to restore judicial independence have enjoyed broad European support. Declining to defend him, meanwhile, could raise uncomfortable questions about why political pressure on central bankers is unacceptable in Washington but potentially permissible in Warsaw.

There are important legal distinctions between these cases. Allegations of misconduct must be distinguished from political disagreement about monetary policy. The question is whether European institutions can maintain that distinction when the domestic authorities responsible for adjudicating it disagree about which laws and judgments are binding.

For the ECB, this is more than a Polish constitutional curiosity.

Its credibility depends on the perception that monetary rules are applied consistently, particularly at a time when the fiscal strains of major eurozone economies are testing the boundaries between monetary independence and government financing.

A dispute that leaves European institutions appearing to choose between competing political authorities could weaken that perception, regardless of the legal merits.

There is no inevitability about a crisis. Parliament may delay its vote, appointments may resolve the management board problem and the legal dispute may be contained before it affects monetary operations.

But Poland exposes a vulnerability that is often overlooked in discussions of central bank independence. Legal safeguards are only as effective as the constitutional consensus that gives them force.

Western policymakers have become accustomed to treating central bank independence as a settled institutional achievement, rather than a political arrangement whose legitimacy ultimately depends on competing authorities agreeing to respect it.

The Polish case may yet demonstrate that the greatest danger is not what policymakers do not know about monetary independence, but what they have come to know for certain that just isn’t so.

data.title: Healey poised to launch raid on banks
data.description:
John Healey is poised to launch a tax raid on banks despite describing financial institutions as “the jewel in the British economic crown”.

The Chancellor is preparing to target lenders in his Budget on Oct 28 as he faces pressure to repair Britain’s public finances.

It comes despite Mr Healey praising banks on Thursday in comments that raised hopes that the City would be spared.

Speaking in Bangkok at an International Monetary Fund (IMF) event on Thursday, the Chancellor said of banks: “They’re a big contributor to the economy.

“They’re an important part of our business. They’re a part of the jewel, if you like, in the British economic crown.”

The Chancellor is said to be considering raising a surcharge on bank profits above £100m from 3pc to 8pc. The move has been advocated by unions and Labour figures, including Angela Rayner, who argue it could raise £2bn for the Treasury.

However, banks have cast doubt on this estimate, warning that such a move would ultimately cost the economy £20bn.

In a letter sent to Mr Healey on Monday, lobby group UK Finance said raising the bank surcharge to 8pc would result in “around £6bn of UK output forgone over the five-year Budget forecast period, rising to nearly £20bn over 10 years”.

David Postings, the chief executive of UK Finance, wrote: “A near-term increase in tax revenue could come at the expense of the lending and investment needed to reindustrialise the economy and drive growth across the UK.”

Shares in Lloyds Banking Group and NatWest both fell around 2pc in early trading on Friday.

Earlier this year, the IMF warned that Britain was reaching the point of peak taxation. It cautioned that the UK faced “economic realities” that left little room for further tax rises or borrowing.

The Chancellor’s plan to target banks, first reported by The Guardian, was met with alarm in the City.

An executive at one of Britain’s biggest banks said: “The impact of a bank tax has a longer burn impact than National Insurance. The impact of a bank tax is about international investability in Britain.”

Another senior banking executive said: “What happens if banks face higher costs? They’ll just pass those costs on.”

Treasury officials have sought to avoid speculation about Mr Healey’s first Budget, citing the turmoil in financial markets in the run-up to Rachel Reeves’s Budget last year.

Journalists and think tank staff have been given less access than usual to the Budget process, while senior Treasury officials have instituted military-grade IT security for staff working on Mr Healey’s statement.

However, Thursday’s apparent about-turn on bank taxes bucked the trend, despite attempts by Treasury sources to shut down speculation about the Chancellor’s plans.

Some officials have complained that the Budget-writing process has been conducted later than usual because of Mr Healey’s recent appointment to the Treasury and desire to ensure his decisions align with Andy Burnham’s priorities in No 10.

Speaking in Bangkok, Mr Healey warned that Britain faced a “tough time” before the Budget amid rising borrowing costs and slowing growth.

He was speaking after official figures showed the UK economy grew by just 0.1pc in August, slowing from 0.4pc in July.

The Chancellor promised to deliver more “breathing space” for households and businesses on Oct 28. However, he cautioned that the economic backdrop limited what was possible.

Mr Healey told the BBC: “It’s a tough time ... People can see the global economic conflicts. They know the pressure it is putting on them. People recognise these times are tough for everyone.”

Heavy spending on AI was the only thing that saved the economy from contracting in August, according to official data published on Thursday. However, AI companies have been hit by a sell-off of their stocks and bonds in recent days, underlining the risks to this boom.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Britain needs growth. But a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it. Labour should be backing businesses and wealth-creators, not making their lives even harder. Rather than hiking taxes yet again, Labour should cut spending.”

Higher inflation and borrowing costs since the outbreak of the war in Iran have put pressure on the public finances, with Mr Healey expected to run down some of the £24bn buffer his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, built last year to help to balance the books.

The Chancellor reiterated his commitment to abide by the fiscal rules set by Ms Reeves, and signalled that it was the “job” of government departments to play their part by tightening their belts.

Mr Healey said: “There are pressures on departments… but it’s important that they do manage within what they’ve got, it’s part of the job. You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things or more of the same.”

The Chancellor made the remarks after Andy Burnham rejected pleas from Yvette Cooper, the Health Secretary, to top up NHS budgets.

Mr Healey added: “I’ve said from day one and week one, and I’ve had Andy Burnham in lockstep alongside me: I will meet those fiscal rules in full.”

Asked whether he would offer more support with the cost of living in the Budget, the Chancellor highlighted that the Government had already taken VAT off energy bills.

“It doesn’t remove the cost pressure,” he said. “It recognises those pressures and says, look, where we can, we’re a government that will act to try and give people a bit of breathing space.”

The Chancellor is drawing up plans for fresh energy support for struggling households, as well as tax cuts for high-street businesses.

Mr Healey said the Government recognised that support was needed for “the cost of business, not just the cost of living”.

He added: “I want the Budget to be a Budget that gives Britain a bit of breathing space, but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans and the strength of our resilience of our economy for the future.”

A Treasury spokesman said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the Chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

data.title: IMF: Healey should cut welfare spending instead of taxing banks
data.description:
John Healey should focus on cutting welfare rather than imposing a bank tax to balance the books, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

The fund warned that Labour’s repeated tax raids were delivering diminishing returns and called for a renewed focus on spending cuts to limit the damage to the economy.

The IMF has weighed into the debate about Britain’s public finances after it emerged that the Chancellor was preparing a raid on banks in the Budget, despite describing them as “the jewel in the British economic crown”.

Mr Healey is said to be considering raising the surcharge on bank profits above £100m from 3pc to 8pc to help fund cost of living support for struggling households.

However, Helge Berger, a director in the IMF’s European department, said balancing tax rises with spending cuts “makes good sense”.

Asked for his views on a potential bank tax, Mr Berger pointed to the need to better target public spending.

He said: “Removing the triple lock, better targeting social benefits are there, so I think that’s where we would put the emphasis rather than on the tax that you mentioned.”

Asked whether welfare spending should be cut back, Mr Berger said: “Achieving good results or even better results with less money is probably a good way of doing it.”

The total welfare bill is on course to top £400bn by the end of the decade. Meanwhile, fresh IMF forecasts published this week showed that Britain was raising taxes at the fastest pace in the West.

Mr Berger said: “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40pc of GDP, that’s historically for Britain a high number.”

The banking sector is anticipating a tax raid after earnings were boosted by higher interest rates caused by the Iran war.

The Chancellor described the banking sector as the “jewel in the British economic crown” on Thursday, but warned he had “decisions to take” in the Budget on Oct 28.

Figures in the City criticised the prospect of a bank tax, which sent shares of NatWest and Lloyds Banking Group down more than 2pc on Friday. Both are heavily exposed to the UK economy.

Sir Philip Hampton, the City grandee and a former chairman of RBS, said it would mean Mr Healey was taxing banks to fund welfare payments.

He said: “If they do it, it would be consistent with the familiar approach to tax business to support the growth in welfare payments. That was the key feature of the 2024 Budget.”

Sir Philip added that bank profits are cyclical, often rising and falling with interest rates.

He said: “If they pay ‘windfall’ taxes in good times but don’t get tax easing when the cycle moves against them, over time their profits and so ability [their] to lend will be distorted and reduced.”

He added: “Banks are doing quite well from rising rates and they are a popular target politically.

“But as a recurring theme, business taxes, especially when they are variable or even capricious, tends to reduce growth and increase unemployment.”

UBS warned a bank tax would drive up mortgage rates and worsen the cost of living crisis, as banks pass on the burden of higher taxes to customers by raising borrowing costs.

Jason Napier, an analyst, warned that a raid on banks would also “disincentivise” investment and “bring in less money than moves the needle” on public spending and debt.

Jamie Dimon, the boss of JP Morgan, warned earlier this year that his bank could pull investment from the UK if the Government chose to “become hostile to banks again”.

A City chief executive said: “Yet again, UK plc puts up a massive sign saying ‘foreign capital not welcome here’.

“Major banks can choose where to deploy their capital, and the UK does not have a divine right to that capital – it will simply go elsewhere.

“Burnham and Healey swerve the difficult political issue of reducing the welfare bill, but instead raise taxes, [this] will hurt the economy and then make the welfare bill even more unaffordable.”

Separately, the Chancellor is said to be considering the launch of a new visa route for wealthy foreigners in the Budget, after the exodus of several high-profile business people and entrepreneurs from the UK.

Christopher Rokos, the hedge fund tycoon and philanthropist, Guillaume Pousaz, the founder of Checkout.com, and Nassef Sawiri, Egypt’s second richest person, have all quit Britain since Labour took office.

Mr Healey’s move to consider a new investor visa in the Budget, which was first reported by Bloomberg, would be seen as an attempt to stem the flow of wealthy individuals leaving the UK.

data.title: Households risk higher energy bills to protect suppliers from collapse
data.description:
Households could face higher energy bills to protect gas and electricity suppliers from collapse.

Under new rules proposed by Ofgem, the energy industry regulator, suppliers would be obliged to pay rivals if they lure customers away with cheaper deals.

The rules are intended to stop another wave of suppliers collapsing, as happened in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

However, the proposals have been criticised by financial campaigners, who warned that switching penalties would ultimately be passed on to customers in the form of higher bills.

Ofgem wants to make it more expensive to change suppliers to reduce the risk of an exodus of customers if a company’s prices are undercut by competitors.

The regulator’s fear is that although energy prices are now high because of the Iran conflict, they are likely to plummet when the war ends or supplies ease. This would be a welcome move for consumers but could spell disaster for some suppliers.

UK suppliers are encouraged to “hedge” by buying gas in advance. However, those with fewer hedging contracts would be able to cut prices to encourage customers to switch.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem’s markets director, said the aim was to protect consumers from volatile global prices: “We’re preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households.

“While the energy market is stronger than it was during the energy crisis, volatility remains ... It’s important that suppliers can continue to secure the energy their customers need without taking unsustainable risks.”

Ofgem’s “market stability charge” would see any firm taking on a new customer, including on a cheap fix or other specialist tariff, forced to pay compensation to that customer’s old supplier.

Martin Lewis, founder of the Money Saving Expert service, warned that the move would raise prices for consumers.

“In a nutshell, it means if wholesale energy prices drop sharply, the cheap fixes and switcher’s deals offered will be a lot more expensive, in order to protect energy firms’ profits,” he said.

“That’s because any firm taking on a new customer, including on a cheap fix or other specialist tariff, will have to pay compensation to that customer’s old supplier, if they switch. It’s basically a form of switching penalty.

“While technically this is a consultation, it’s one of those where Ofgem has made up its mind, but is required to consult – it will almost certainly happen.”

Ofgem’s move comes despite growing concern about the impact of high energy prices on low-income households. Energy debts are estimated at £7bn by Energy UK and there are increasing calls for the forthcoming Budget to tackle the problem.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, are reportedly considering measures such as a temporary expansion of the Warm Home Discount, potentially raising the annual rebate from £150 to £250 for each qualifying household for the 2026-27 winter period.

Gillian Cooper, at Citizens Advice, said the wider problem was simply the very high energy prices hitting UK consumers.

She said: “Bringing back the market stabilisation charge is a warning sign that energy prices are back in dangerous territory.

“The Government must recognise this for what it is: a warning that prices are rocketing and urgent winter crisis support is essential. At the Budget, we need a clear plan to deliver targeted bill support to those most at risk before they are pushed over the brink.”

data.title: Hundreds of pharmacies face closure from Labour tax raid
data.description:
Hundreds of pharmacies are facing closure because of soaring business rates, with owners warning that high taxes are forcing them to cut services for vulnerable patients.

Almost half of the 420 pharmacy owners surveyed by the National Pharmacy Association (NPA) said they were considering shutting down their practices because of higher business rates bills.

The trade body warned that pharmacies, many of which are family-run businesses, are unable to offset the higher tax burden by raising prices, which are fixed by the NHS.

The NPA found 55pc of pharmacy operators were considering moving to cheaper premises, raising fears that some rural and coastal communities could be left without a local branch.

Andy Burnham has made lowering business rates for high-street businesses a key pillar of his summer policy blitz, announcing a 20pc reduction for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April next year.

However, pharmacies have been excluded from the relief.

The tax squeeze has intensified since business rates were increased for many properties after Rachel Reeves’s second Budget. Bills have also been affected by the latest revaluation of commercial property.

GPs and NHS dentists, meanwhile, have their business rates reimbursed.

Pharmacies are particularly exposed because most of their income comes from the NHS, meaning they cannot simply raise prices to cover higher costs. Roughly 90pc of pharmacies’ income comes from the health service, the NPA said.

Onkar Singh, who runs 20 pharmacies across the Black Country, Staffordshire, Herefordshire and Worcestershire, has seen his business rates bill rise by roughly 20pc to 30pc in the past year. His total bill is now about £250,000.

He has closed two of his pharmacies in the past two years and reduced opening hours across virtually his entire estate. He has also been forced to cut back services, such as offering free medicine deliveries to elderly patients.

Mr Singh said: “The last three years have been the worst period in my 30 years of pharmacy.

“People are having to close a lifetime’s worth of work and effort, and having to close or reduce hours or dip into their pension pot just to keep going for their communities.”

The NPA survey found that 92pc of pharmacies said their rates bill was preventing them from investing in their workforce or renovations. Some pharmacists have warned that their bills have tripled.

Mr Singh said the impact was particularly painful because pharmacies were often being asked to fill gaps elsewhere in the NHS.

He said: “It is frustrating that pubs and restaurants get the headlines, but pharmacies are actually delivering care.

“The NHS accepted that pharmacy did an exceptional job, but in terms of funding and support with business rates we seem to be forgotten.”

The NPA said 44 pharmacies had already closed this year, leaving the national network at its smallest since 2006.

Nine in 10 council areas have lost at least one pharmacy since 2022.

Olivier Picard, the chairman of the trade group, said pharmacies should receive the same rates treatment as GPs and dentists, arguing that they provide an essential health service.

A government spokesperson said: “Pharmacies already benefit from our wider business rates reforms, including permanently lower multipliers and our £4.3bn package to support ratepayers – and the government has increased funding for the sector by £340m this year as part of our shift to bring care closer to home.”

data.title: The West is hooked on Chinese drugs but they could save your life
data.description:
Sir Keir Starmer’s decision to invite Sir Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca’s chief executive, to Beijing at the beginning of the year was a textbook piece of modern diplomacy.

The then-prime minister’s attempt to revive economic cooperation rested on a knockout deal that went beyond the usual warm words. Sir Pascal, a sworn Sinophile and one of the biggest cheerleaders of Chinese innovation, was only too happy to oblige.

Within hours of Sir Keir’s arrival, AstraZeneca had unveiled a plan to invest $15bn (£11bn) in China, building on its existing medical manufacturing and research capabilities in Beijing, Shanghai, Wuxi, Taizhou and Qingdao.

AstraZeneca’s pledge was the marquee announcement of Sir Keir’s trip. Sir Pascal said the “landmark investment” marked the next chapter for the company in China. For the politburo, it was further proof that their plan to turn China into a global pharmaceuticals leader has worked.

In the West, China has long been dismissed as little more than a dealer in cheap copycat medicines – both legal and illegal – and increasingly knockoffs too, such as unlicensed GLP-1 weight loss medication.

This portrayal no longer bears scrutiny, however. In recent years, the Chinese pharmaceutical industry has undergone a remarkable reinvention. Western industry leaders view it as a bona fide drug superpower at the forefront of discovery.

China controls an exciting pipeline of groundbreaking medicines and occupies a growing role as a globally important venue for clinical trials.

But for now, cooperation between East and West suits both sides. European and American drugmakers have rushed to embrace Chinese research, forging multi-billion licensing deals. Those with the appetite have opened their own labs and even set up manufacturing outposts.

Chinese science is now “the best in the world” and ignoring it is not an option, says one European pharmaceuticals chairman.

Few have led the charge as enthusiastically as Sir Pascal, AstraZeneca’s swashbuckling French boss. China is now its second-biggest market. Meanwhile GSK, the UK’s other national drug champion, has struck a series of partnerships with Chinese labs to licence promising drugs outside the country.

These relationships are critical for China’s pharmaceuticals industry, providing access to the lucrative markets that fund innovation. At home, their only customer is Xi Jinping, and he sets the price.

Yet this partnership is fragile. Amid growing concern in the US about the threat China’s new scientific prowess poses to drug supplies, innovation and even national security, industry executives fear an iron curtain will be drawn.

Drugs may be the next front in the superpower trade war that has already drawn in telecoms equipment, semiconductors, electric vehicles, rare earth minerals and solar panels.

For Europe, including Britain’s pharmaceutical giants AstraZeneca and GSK, the looming nightmare is that an American administration will sooner or later use its economic muscle to effectively outlaw their cooperation with China.

One senior figure says the possibility of a sweeping American crackdown is “probably the one question that keeps me awake at night”.

China’s rapid scientific progress

Dr Zhao Hong, a renowned Chinese cancer specialist, shocked thousands of Communist Party delegates in March last year: a Guangzhou-based biotech firm had developed a cancer drug that had outperformed the world’s bestselling equivalent in clinical trials.

The work of China’s Akeso Biopharma, lung cancer drug ivonescimab had shown that it could delay non-small-cell lung cancer progression for five months longer than US giant Merck’s Keytruda treatment – the world’s bestselling prescription drug in 2025.

The success of ivonescimab was hailed as a breakthrough moment for China’s pharmaceutical industry.

“China is at the best time of its biopharmaceutical sector’s development,” Hong told state media at the annual Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference.

The speed with which China is catching up in pharmaceuticals and biotech is astonishing.

By 2024, China had 1,255 drugs at the research stage, a nearly eight-fold jump in less than a decade. America had 1,441 – a 15pc rise – while the total in Europe had shrunk slightly to 400.

Experts attribute the leap to a fundamental shift in how the industry was perceived by the Chinese regime.

One veteran UK executive recalls how when he first used to visit China in the late 1990s, it was to complain about “counterfeits and pharmaceuticals that were really dangerous”. Today, China is seen as “a golden opportunity”, he says.

“They have moved deliberately to be at the leading edge of science,” he adds.

Beijing has provided vast support in the form of scores of state-financed biotechnology parks equipped with advanced laboratories and heavily subsidised hardware, together with a sweeping overhaul of the regulatory system beginning in 2015.

A study by Prof Yimin Cui, of Peking University, and colleagues found that the time taken to approve a drug for human trials fell to 87 days after the reforms, from 501 days previously.

Chinese researchers are helped by the sheer size of the country’s population – last counted at more than 1.4 billion – says Freddy Yip, a corporate lawyer at Cooley.

“In the US, it may take a long time to recruit sufficient patients, but in China, you have access to lots of different patients with different kinds of diseases, including many rare diseases,” Yip says.

Sir Pascal has said this combination of scientific capability and rapid execution – “China speed”, as he has called it – can help to dramatically accelerate drug development.

One of China’s leading biotech venture capitalists estimates clinical trials are “two thirds cheaper and half as quick in China”.

Progress has been spurred by a massive increase in spending on research and development – leaping from $35m in 2015 to $15bn in 2023 – and a “reverse brain drain” in which thousands of foreign-educated Chinese scientists and entrepreneurs have returned home, according to Porsche Consulting.

Chinese scientists are now at the vanguard of treatment for cardiovascular diseases and cancer, as well as spearheading drug development for metabolic conditions and neurological disorders, such as Parkinson’s, among many others.

Alarm bells in Washington

Mere months before Sir Pascal was lending heft to Sir Keir’s Beijing bridge-building mission, the Frenchman was being warmly welcomed at the Oval Office by Donald Trump.

Thanking the US president for welcoming him “in this beautiful office”, Sir Pascal was armed with another crowd-pleasing announcement: a pledge to cut drug prescription prices in the US, after Trump had accused other countries of “freeloading” at the expense of Americans.

Sir Pascal went further as well, unveiling a $50bn plan to expand the company’s existing operations in the US. In return, AstraZeneca received a three-year exemption from tariffs.

Privately, AstraZeneca executives acknowledge it was also an attempt to ward off growing concern in the White House about the deepening of ties with China.

“We are cognisant of some of the more hawkish commentary [from US politicians]. It is a delicate balancing act, and we are treading a fine line by recognising what the US is trying to achieve,” an insider says.

Yet, for all Washington’s alarm, dependency has become more pronounced, not less. Western companies have piled into the country, hoovering up clinical trial data and striking licensing deals to develop Chinese medicines outside the mainland, which they hope can then be used to treat patients across the developed world.

“This is the golden age of science and China is white-hot right now,” an industry source says.

Deal activity is being driven by anxiety among European and US companies as their pipeline of drugs peters out.

America’s biotech industry faces the alarming prospect of an estimated $350bn worth of medicines – equivalent to roughly one fifth of projected global prescription-drug revenue – losing patent protection by the end of the decade.

When patents run out, generic rivals are allowed to gatecrash the market, jeopardising sales.

Few have led the way with the verve that AstraZeneca has demonstrated.

Sir Pascal’s Beijing announcement was accompanied by a boast that it had signed 16 global licensing agreements with 15 Chinese partners since 2023 alone – thought to be the most of any overseas pharmaceuticals multi-national.

GSK hasn’t been far behind. Last year, the company struck an alliance with local giant Hengrui Pharma to develop a dozen new medicines outside the mainland. The value of the deal could eventually total $12bn.

The agreements are part of an industry-wide surge in deals totalling $138bn last year – a nearly tenfold jump since 2021 – according to data provider PharmCube. 2026 is expected to be another record.

Deal flow shows little sign of slowing.

A fortnight ago, GSK unveiled a $1.3bn pact with Hutchmed, a Hong Kong-based biopharmaceuticals company with research facilities in Shanghai, for the bulk of the licensing rights to what it called “first in-class” cancer treatments.

Brewing geopolitical storm

Amid the feeding frenzy, concern in Washington has turned to outright hostility in some quarters.

In December last year, Trump signed into law the Biosecure Act, a move widely seen as a sharp escalation in tensions and the moment the longstanding strategic rivalry between the US and China spilt into the biotechnology arena.

The act prevents US companies reliant on federal contracts and funding from working with Chinese biotech firms with ties to the Chinese military and any deemed to pose a national security risk. It also bars Chinese companies from accessing US government funding themselves.

US biotechnology companies with federal contracts are now engaged in a mad dash to purge their supply chains of equipment obtained from any Chinese biotechnology firms on the banned list.

Next up is the Biotech Investment National Security Act. Though not yet signed into law, it will subject licensing deals involving Chinese companies to national security reviews.

Though technically a screening mechanism rather than a ban on licensing Chinese drugs, it will effectively function as one, says Craig Garthwaite, a professor at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

There is also pressure to bar the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) from accepting Chinese trial data, amid concerns about their reliability. The FDA has repeatedly rejected one of Hengrui’s cancer drugs, citing questions about quality control at its manufacturing sites.

As one senior City figure puts it: the White House has conjured up other reasons to “erect a wall around China”.

AstraZeneca’s attempt to navigate this geopolitical storm by investing in both China and the US divides opinion. Some see it as an inspired way to keep both Washington and Beijing happy at the same time.

“I think Pascal has been very smart in not allowing anybody to question his US credentials. He’s playing his cards very wisely,” the boss of a rival company says.

Others see it as a high-stakes gamble from a company that is more exposed than most of its competitors and has learnt the hard way the risks that come from operating in China.

Leon Wang, the former head of its Chinese operations, is awaiting trial on charges of illegal trading, unlawful collection of personal information and medical insurance fraud, alongside another former employee, having been arrested in 2024.

If the saga made Sir Pascal reconsider his appetite for doing business in China, there is little sign of it.

Alongside licensing deals potentially worth tens of billions of dollars, it has around 17,000 employees in China, two “global strategic” research and development centres in Beijing and Shanghai, and four advanced manufacturing sites in Wuxi, Taizhou, Qingdao and Beijing.

China is now AstraZeneca’s second-largest market after the US, accounting for roughly 12pc of the company’s global turnover, and its Chinese facilities supply more than 70 markets worldwide.

In a written submission to the Commons business and trade select committee in July, AstraZeneca described co-operation with China as a “win-win”.

But as one investor with extensive interests in China points out: “If you’re a big pharma company with a significant proportion of your licensing spend coming from China and the tap suddenly gets turned off, that’s obviously a problem.”

Europe’s wary response

Despite sharply rising tensions, there are concerns that European policymakers are still a long way off from having a coherent industrial strategy that addresses the China question.

Having been slow to react to the threat that cheap Chinese manufacturing poses to the continent’s steelmakers, solar panel producers and its car industry, the risk is that the pendulum swings too far the other way and Brussels takes a similarly antagonistic approach in trying to shut China out of other sectors, such as pharmaceuticals.

Calls by Oliver Blume, the chief executive of Volkswagen, for tougher trade measures against Beijing have been interpreted in some circles as a signal that EU-China relations are close to a tipping point after years of resistance to anti-Chinese duties from the continent’s car giants.

Yet, a senior industrialist says Europe lacks the “economic counterweight to be able to exclude China”.

“I don’t necessarily think it’s good in the long term for the US to do so, but I think it’s very dangerous for Europe,” he adds.

“We need a more nuanced industrial strategy that seeks Chinese expertise and cost effectiveness, and to somehow bring some of the economic benefit of that into Europe,” he says.

Such sentiment echoes a growing willingness among car manufacturers to partner with Chinese counterparts amid an onslaught of imports. Nissan’s decision to share its Sunderland plant with Chery, one of China’s largest car exporters, is expected to be among the first of many similar tie-ups.

Some believe the growing divide between Washington and Beijing because of pharmaceuticals may even present an opportunity for Europe.

“I’m sure Europe would be more than happy to take Chinese-developed products that are sold to them at a lower price than what they might otherwise get from the United States,” Garthwaite says.

As Brussels bureaucrats try to agree on a co-ordinated approach, the rhetoric, particularly among some influential Republicans, continues to harden.

Chris Klomp, a top lieutenant of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, has likened the situation to “a war”.

Anxiety has been heightened by a so-called “hot mic” incident at a Beijing military parade late last year, in which Vladimir Putin and Xi were overheard discussing the possibility that humans could live to 150 years old, thanks to advances in biotechnology.

Some China hawks saw it as further evidence that the US risked falling behind in the global race for domination in advanced science.

The Council on Foreign Relations, an influential American think tank, has called for reliance on China’s biotech know-how to be treated as a strategic vulnerability akin to critical minerals.

“The US (and just about every other nation) faces a growing risk that China will deliberately withhold essential pharmaceutical inputs as a tool of economic or political coercion … as China has done with rare-earth critical minerals,” it warned in June.

The Atlantic Council, another US think tank with a history of shaping American foreign policy, points out that the US is reliant on China for three quarters of some imported drugs and as much as 99pc of some raw materials that are critical to the production of certain key medicines.

What’s more, China’s 2020 export control law and 2021 biosecurity law “grant broad authority to weaponise pharmaceutical exports”, it said recently.

‘All in or all out’

AstraZeneca declined to comment on its position, but there are signs it is more nervous than it is willing to acknowledge.

It emerged in August that the company had held detailed discussions with American rival Bristol Myers Squibb about a potential £300bn mega-merger.

In seeking to substantially deepen its US footprint, AstraZeneca may have concluded that the best chance it has of escaping any crackdown is if the company can demonstrate it is willing to take action to address Trump’s demands for the “reshoring” of pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Radical corporate restructuring plans have also been explored in China. AstraZeneca previously looked at the possibility of carving out its Chinese business into a separate legal entity and listing it on the Shanghai stock exchange. Though nothing came of those plans, they were seen as an attempt to insulate it from mounting geopolitical tensions.

GSK, meanwhile, sees no reason for such drastic action. Publicly, all a spokesman is willing to say is that it has “a longstanding presence in China, to make sure patients can access our medicines and vaccines”.

“China is also increasingly a source of cutting-edge biopharma innovation, and we have established several important collaborations for potential new treatments in oncology, respiratory, immunology and inflammation,” the spokesman adds.

However, like AstraZeneca, it too has fallen foul of Beijing after the company was engulfed in a bribery scandal in 2014.

GSK was found guilty of bribing Chinese doctors and hospitals to prescribe its medical products and was forced to pay a record $490m fine.

That ordeal prompted GSK bosses to take a much more cautious approach in which its activities were limited to strict licensing deals rather than the asset-heavy approach of others, such as AstraZeneca.

“It [GSK] went through a very difficult time in China. The experience damaged the company immeasurably in terms of its willingness to take risks,” a City source says.

By focusing on developing local collaborations, GSK believes it can still capitalise on the opportunities in China while being “less vulnerable” than rivals who are more “asset-exposed”, an insider explains.

Yet, the same person admits it ultimately boils down to one question: “Are they [China] helping us long-term or are they harming us? And I can’t answer that, which is why we can’t afford to be all in or all out.”

Industry figures hope common sense prevails between the two superpowers.

Garthwaite acknowledges deals that come with potential national security risk should be scrutinised, while attempts to reduce American over-dependence on Chinese antibiotics are also to be applauded.

However, he says the White House needs to distinguish between drug production and drug development, which “shouldn’t be too hard”.

Another investor says patients don’t really care where the drugs come from, “as long as they’re subjected to the same trials”.

In response to a recent US ban on imports of humanoid robots, China’s foreign ministry said: “Protectionism does not make the US more competitive … it will only hurt the interests of US companies and consumers.”﻿

Yet, nor is it in China’s interests to actively undermine American science. Chinese drugmakers simply cannot afford to be shut out of Western markets, particularly the US, experts say.

“China is really vulnerable too. It has to rely on its export machine because it doesn’t have sufficient levels of internal consumption,” one analyst says.

Ultimately, industry sources admit they are at the mercy of an unpredictable Trump administration whose appetite for trade wars shows little sign of waning.

As one boardroom veteran puts it: “It’s akin to walking a tightrope – we’ll continue trying to walk it and hope we stay on.”

data.title: Second-class stamp price rises capped after Royal Mail’s delivery failures
data.description:
Royal Mail is to be blocked from raising second-class stamp prices ahead of inflation after its “unacceptable” failure to meet delivery targets.

Ofcom, the communications regulator, has proposed extending its cap on raising the price of second-class stamps by more than inflation until March 2028.

The move comes after Royal Mail increased stamp prices seven times in four years, with first-class postage almost doubling since 2022. Ofcom does not cap first-class stamp prices, leaving Royal Mail free to keep raising them.

Ofcom said it was extending the price cap as Royal Mail reforms its universal service obligation and “improves its delivery performance, which has been unacceptable in recent years”.

Fergal Farragher, Ofcom’s policy director, said: “The number of letters being sent is declining and Royal Mail’s financial position is stark, which is why we reformed its universal service obligations last year.

“The company is now making some progress with its universal service reforms and improvements to its delivery performance, which has been unacceptable in recent years.”

A first-class stamp now costs £1.80, compared with just 95p in 2022 and 63p in 2015. Second-class stamps have also become more expensive, rising from 87p to 91p in April.

Ofcom’s proposals would allow second-class prices to rise in line with inflation for another year, rather than imposing an outright freeze.

Citizens Advice accused the regulator of letting Royal Mail “off the hook” by failing to extend the price caps to first-class stamps.

Tom MacInnes, the charity’s director of policy, said: “The regulator could’ve seized this opportunity to extend price caps to first class stamps, and make any future price rises explicitly conditional on the company hitting its now-reduced delivery targets, but didn’t.

“Ofcom is kicking the can down the road, leaving consumers again waiting for a reliable and affordable postal service.”

The intervention follows years of complaints about Royal Mail’s poor service, with customers paying more despite millions of letters arriving late.

The company delivered just 75.7pc of first-class letters on time in the year to March, against a target of 93pc.

Only 90.2pc of second-class letters arrived within three working days, compared with a target of 98.5pc.

It has not met its first-class delivery targets since 2017, while second-class performance has fallen short for six years.

Royal Mail was fined £21m last October for missing delivery targets, taking its penalties over three years to more than £36m.

Ofcom said the company had been too slow to introduce reforms designed to improve reliability and cut costs.

Royal Mail was bought last year by Daniel Křetínský, a Czech billionaire.

It has since been allowed to scrap Saturday second-class letter deliveries and switch to delivering on alternate weekdays as part of reforms to the universal service obligation.

Ofcom estimates the changes could save Royal Mail between £250m and £425m a year, although their introduction has been delayed.

Royal Mail has blamed rising delivery costs and a 70pc decline in letter volumes over two decades for higher prices.

Ofcom will make a final decision on the proposed extension before the existing cap expires next March.

Royal Mail accused Ofcom of dragging its feet over stamp prices, warning that falling letter volumes were threatening the future of the postal service.

A spokesman said: “Ofcom’s announcement today recognises the substantial decline in letter volumes is threatening the sustainability of the universal postal service, frustratingly yet again it has delayed its decision on one of the key actions needed to address it.”

data.title: Johnson & Johnson offers £4.1bn to settle talcum powder cancer claims
data.description:
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) has agreed to pay an estimated $5.5bn (£4.1bn) to resolve tens of thousands of claims that its baby powder caused ovarian cancer.

The pharmaceutical giant’s offer of a settlement could end a decade-long legal battle that has dogged the company.

Erik Haas, vice-president of litigation at J&J, said the claims that its talcum powder products caused cancer were “meritless” ‌but said the company was willing ⁠to settle to get closure.

The settlement covers around 76,000 claims and must be accepted by 95pc of the ovarian cancer claimants in state or federal court before it becomes final.

J&J previously settled the majority of cases alleging that its talc contained asbestos and caused mesothelioma, a rare but aggressive cancer affected the lungs, abdomen or heart.

Mr Haas said: “While we are confident the company would have ultimately prevailed with further litigation, as it has in the vast majority of cases tried to date, this resolution allows the company to put this matter behind it and remain focused on its mission to develop medicines and devices that save ⁠lives.”

J&J expects to pay $3bn in 2027, and it will make further payments in 2028.

More than 3,000 people filed lawsuits at Britain’s High Court last year alleging that either they or a family member developed ovarian cancer or mesothelioma as a result of using Johnson’s Baby Powder between 1965 and 2023.

The settlements announced on Monday included groups who filed claims in federal and state courts.

J&J ended global sales of baby powder containing the mineral talc in 2023, switching to a formulation based on corn starch.

The settlements come after cases were put on hold for more than three years after a series of bankruptcy filings by J&J.

It filed three bankruptcies through a shell-company subsidiary in an ‌effort to settle the cases. Each bankruptcy ended in dismissal and the litigation resumed in March 2025.

Chris Seeger, an attorney who represents about 2,500 clients with talc claims and helped negotiate the agreement, said J&J could ultimately pay $7bn or more.

The settlement assigns specific values to qualifying ovarian cancer claims but does not cap J&J’s total payout.

He said: “We got ‌a fair settlement, and our clients are going to be happy with it.”

data.title: Households face debt ‘doom loop’ as energy bills rise
data.description:
Households face a debt “doom loop” as energy bills rise, the chief executive of Scottish Power has warned.

Keith Anderson said that debts from household gas and electricity bills will hit at least £7bn next year, forcing suppliers to recoup more costs from those who are able to pay.

This crisis will only worsen as prices rise, Mr Anderson said, with EDF warning that energy bills will jump from £1,723 today to more than £2,204 next April.

Unpaid energy debts are already adding £67 a year to the average bill under rules set by Ofgem, the regulator. However, this is poised to hit £100 if debts keep rising.

Speaking at an industry conference on Wednesday, Mr Anderson said: “Everybody thinks energy debt is headed towards £7bn, and even then there’s no end in sight.

“It’s one of the biggest challenges facing this industry, and we failed to grapple it, and we failed to get on top of it.

“Collectively, the industry has been unable to support customers, so we’re reaching a point now where that debt burden is neither fair to those who are paying, and it’s not sustainable for the companies carrying it.

“If we’re serious about affordability in the long term, we have to be serious about tackling that debt issue.

“We’re heading into a doom loop of asking today’s bill-payers to pick up the costs of others without solving any of the issues that caused it.”

Similar concerns have also been raised in the water sector, where debts could hit £3bn by next year, according to James Cooper from energy consultancy Baringa.

He said: “We could realistically be talking about £10bn of household debt in utilities within 18 months, which is a frightening figure.

“At that sort of level for energy, we will be looking at just shy of £100 for the average bill of paying households to cover the cost of that debt.”

Debts in the energy industry have largely been blamed on rising bills, which have been driven up by green levies and fallout from the Iran war.

Wholesale gas prices hit their highest levels since 2022 on Wednesday at 217p per therm, up from just 81p a year ago.

This has increased pressure on Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, to approve the UK’s Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gas fields, which could boost energy output by up to 10pc.

She said on Wednesday that a decision on whether to give Jackdaw the green light was “imminent”.

An announcement is expected as early as next week but a decision on Rosebank, the largest untapped oil field in UK waters, will take “a bit longer”, she said.

She also stressed that the UK was not at risk of blackouts this winter.

“I’m 100pc confident that [the lights] won’t go out this winter,” she said. “The first duty of the Secretary of State is to make sure that we can deliver security supply.

“So that is the first question I’ve asked of the system, and we tested it and we kicked it round, and I am 100pc confident. We haven’t had an outage or problems [nationally] with security supply for coming on for 20 years.”

data.title: Richard Branson: Trump is appeasing dictators and autocrats
data.description:
Sir Richard Branson has accused Donald Trump of being “an appeaser to autocrats and dictators”.

The outspoken Virgin Group founder criticised Mr Trump on LinkedIn in response to reports that the US president had blocked Ukraine from the Pentagon’s Starshield system, a critical defensive and battlefield support system.

The British billionaire wrote: “The Trump administration has become an appeaser to autocrats and dictators, putting their personal whims before the best interests of the American people and those of the free world.

“How will America’s allies ever be able to trust this administration again, when they are now turning against them at a time of war and suffering?”

Sir Richard is among just a handful of corporate executives who have been prepared to criticise Mr Trump publicly, and has been escalating his attacks this week.

In a series of posts this week, he criticised both Mr Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin and also the US president’s subsequent verbal attacks on Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s leader.

On Monday, he described Mr Trump’s deal with Putin for 1.8 million tonnes of Russian diesel as “the most astonishing act of hypocrisy I’ve seen in my lifetime, and I’ve been around for 76 years”.

Sir Richard claimed the hypocrisy lay in the fact that Mr Trump only last month signed into law a policy that allowed Washington to impose tariffs on other countries that bought Russian or Iranian oil.

He also said the White House’s gradual loss of interest in Ukraine had evolved into “a bloody backstabbing”.

He said on Tuesday that Mr Trump’s comments on Mr Zelensky’s culpability for the war were “beyond belief”. On Thursday, he warned that “the free world” could be “dismantled before our very eyes”.

Sir Richard regularly airs his views on political issues, particularly on climate change. More recently he has advocated closer relations between Britain and the EU.

But he is almost alone among executives in launching such scathing attacks on Mr Trump.

Jamie Dimon, the boss of JP Morgan Chase, has occasionally spoken in favour of policies that challenge the White House. He has backed the independence of the US Federal Reserve and recently proposed building “a big, beautiful relationship” with the EU.

Albert Bourla, the boss of Pfizer, has meanwhile criticised the views of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on vaccinations.

But few directly attack Mr Trump’s decisions for fear of retribution.

Chrystia Freeland, the former Canadian deputy prime minister, wrote in the Financial Times on Friday that if Mr Trump suffered defeat in the Nov 3 midterms, it could trigger more open attacks on him from Wall Street corporate titans.

She wrote: “I have had more than a dozen conversations with US CEOs who have apologised to me for their president’s conduct and told me he is hurting America and the world.”

She said many still feared being punished for speaking out but were now poised to move with the herd. 

“Trump’s naked betrayal of Ukraine and open support for Putin could be the last straw,” she said.

The White House was contacted for comment.
