data.title: Mike Ashley tightens grip on Burberry
data.description:
Mike Ashley has tightened his grip on Burberry after upping his stake in the luxury brand, putting him on course to become the group’s biggest shareholder.

The billionaire’s Frasers Group now owns 7.4pc of the trench-coat maker, up from 6.3pc a fortnight ago, after using financial derivatives to add to his holding.

Frasers would become Burberry’s largest investor if Mr Ashley converts the derivatives to shares, a move which would give the fashion tycoon immense power over the 170-year-old fashion brand.

Burberry is worth more than £3.8bn, giving Frasers’ stake a value of about £280m. Mr Ashley’s group originally acquired a 4.2pc stake in the company during the summer.

The fashion house has struggled after an ill-timed push upmarket coincided with a global slowdown in luxury spending.

It reported a £66m loss last year and announced plans to cut 1,700 jobs, although there have been signs of a recovery under Joshua Schulman, its new chief executive.

Sales returned to growth in the three months to June, helped by renewed demand for its signature trench coats.

Burberry is the latest investment for Frasers, which owns Sports Direct and Flannels, after it spent months snapping up stakes in some of the industry’s biggest names.

Last week it unveiled an 8.8pc interest in American sportswear giant Under Armour, a major supplier to Sports Direct.

In August, it bought Harvey Nichols out of administration and has been locked in a bitter battle with the board of German fashion giant Hugo Boss over a potential takeover.

Frasers has amassed an interest of almost 50pc in the brand despite resistance from its leadership. The company also owns around 37pc of Mulberry, the British luxury handbag maker.

Its growing empire is part of a push by Michael Murray, Frasers’ chief executive and Mr Ashley’s son-in-law, to transform the business from a discount sportswear retailer into a major force in luxury fashion.

Last week, Frasers outlined plans to expand its Flannels department store chain across Europe and take the Harvey Nichols brand overseas.

Taking control of Burberry would give Mr Ashley ownership of one of Britain’s most recognisable fashion brands.

Mr Ashley has a history of taking minority stakes in retailers before seeking greater influence over their operations.

Frasers has also built positions in Asos and Boohoo,

However, its investments have not always paid off. Frasers bought luxury retailer Matches in late 2023 but placed it into administration less than three months later.

Burberry declined to comment. Frasers was approached for comment.

data.title: Octopus staff blocked from selling shares in employee fund
data.description:
Octopus employees have been blocked from selling shares in an employee equity scheme.

The investment firm has suspended a planned share sale after it was unable to meet a flood of withdrawal requests.

It marks the latest sign of turmoil at Octopus, which has been battling poor performance at one of its main funds, the Octopus Inheritance Tax Service (OITS).

Nearly 2,000 employees past and present were sent an email by bosses this week informing them of the decision.

The block will apply to a share scheme that is popular with its employees, allowing them to invest up to £150 a month from their gross salary into Octopus Group.

In return, they are granted 1.5 extra shares in the company for free.

As part of the scheme, Octopus runs an internal market where current staff and existing shareholders can buy and sell shares at a liquidity event each year.

However, the firm has now delayed the offer after the share sale was significantly oversubscribed and they were not able to meet the extent of withdrawals.

It comes after Octopus recently offered to waive its annual management charge for both existing and new investors in OITS, missing out on annual fees of around £100m.

The fund had been frozen for nearly three months, coinciding with a failed plan to acquire PlatformX Communications, the wholesale arm of TalkTalk.

However, after the deal collapsed two weeks ago, Octopus Investments said it would split the fund in two.

This led to Octopus permanently gating most of its fibre assets in the fund, which it has acknowledged as the biggest drag on performance.

Octopus said that the rest of the fund, which accounts for just over two thirds of its value, would be reopened. However, it warned that withdrawals could not be guaranteed.

OITS has 18,000 customers and allows investors to lower their inheritance tax bills by investing in businesses to qualify for relief.

Customers of OITS were sold shares in Fern Trading, which owns about 300 energy, property and telecoms companies.

The fund has come under growing scrutiny after The Telegraph revealed that savers had been bankrolling failed hospitals and care homes.

Investors in other Octopus funds have also struggled to get their money back.

Octopus blocked one financial adviser from withdrawing millions of pounds on behalf of his client from one of its schemes for seven months.

Mark Spendlove, of IPP Group, asked Octopus Investments – which manages inheritance tax funds – to withdraw £5.4m from Terido, a scheme aimed at small businesses.

The scheme takes the spare cash from member businesses and invests it in asset-backed loans, mainly in property, ensuring that its investors can qualify for business relief.

Octopus had told Mr Spendlove that the withdrawal process would take about four weeks, but later said that the money would be paid out over seven months, with the final £2m payment not made until March 2027.

OITS has also come under scrutiny for how it has been valuing its assets, particularly after it acknowledged the troubles in its fibre division.

It had previously committed to revaluing the holdings after the acquisition. However, they may not be revalued now until July 2027.

A spokesman for Octopus said: “We’ve always wanted as much of Octopus as possible to be owned by the people who work here, and we’re proud to have created a scheme that gives our employees the opportunity to become shareholders in the business.

“As part of that, since 2013 we’ve held an annual liquidity event which provides a mechanism for shareholders to buy and sell shares in Octopus. It is important to be clear that we haven’t cancelled this year’s event, it is simply delayed until later in the tax year.”

data.title: Channel 5 pays out £215m to US owner Paramount
data.description:
Channel 5’s US parent company Paramount has extracted £215m from the British broadcaster even as it suffered a sharp drop in profits.

The payout, which is among the largest in the channel’s history, was taken from retained earnings in Paramount’s first year under the leadership of David Ellison, the son of Oracle tycoon Larry Ellison.

It came despite Channel 5’s pre-tax profits slumping by two-thirds to £11.9m, while revenues fell 8pc to £292m, according to newly filed accounts.

The All Creatures Great and Small broadcaster blamed the decline on “challenging” conditions in the advertising market as brands continued to divert their spending away from traditional TV.

Channel 5’s travails underscore the challenge facing Mr Ellison, who closed an $8bn (£6bn) deal to take control of Paramount last summer.

He has since pulled off an even more audacious swoop on Warner Bros. The $110bn merger, which closed this week, is set to reshape Hollywood.

But the newly formed company, which has been rebranded Skydance, is already facing questions over eye-watering debt levels.

The company is heavily reliant on its declining linear television business to generate cash to service its debt.

As a result, bosses are also preparing at least $6bn in cost cuts in an effort to balance the books. The dividends suggest Mr Ellison will also squeeze subsidiaries for additional cash.

Channel 5 has previously handed significant dividends to its parent company, including a £740m payout in 2020.

Channel 5, which has an older audience than its rival public-service broadcasters, still attracts much of its viewing through traditional linear TV.

However, the channel has been investing heavily in its streaming service, which relaunched last year under the new brand name “5”.

Bosses said the investment had started to pay off as Channel 5’s streaming viewing rose by more than a third in 2025, outpacing the BBC, ITV and Channel 4.

The company was also boosted by a one-off gain of £19.1m after its investment in a subsidiary was transferred to another part of the Paramount group.

Paramount’s tie-up with Warner Bros, which owns CNN, TNT Sports and the eponymous film studios, has triggered concerns over media plurality and the effect on news provision in the UK.

Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, threatened to intervene in the deal, but ultimately waved it through after Paramount pledged to pump an extra £80m into Channel 5 over the next three years.

The cash will be used to fund news, original children’s programming and an additional 20 hours of drama programming each year.

Channel 5 spent more than £200m on programming last year as it splashed out on new dramas and rights for sports fixtures including the Fifa Club World Cup.

The tournament’s final between Chelsea and Paris St Germain delivered the channel’s biggest ever live sports audience, with a peak of 2.4 million on the main channel and 459,000 streaming it.

Channel 5, which appointed Reemah Sakaan as its new boss at the start of this year, recently struck a deal to shift its £300m advertising sales business from Sky to Channel 4.

Channel 4, which posted a deficit of £10m last year, is also struggling with a decline in the TV ad market and has outlined plans to cut around a quarter of its workforce in the biggest redundancy round in its four-decade history.

data.title: If Amol Rajan wants to be the next Tucker Carlson, he needs people to actually watch him
data.description:
For the first interviewee on his new YouTube channel, Amol Rajan could have done much worse than Sir Gareth Southgate. The former England manager is a household name, widely admired, who has not given many recent interviews. Rajan was fresh off the back of an (admittedly curtailed) appearance on the much-watched Celebrity Traitors. Blockbuster stuff, at least on the team sheet.

But at the time of writing, their two-hour recording had accumulated 3,000 views and 85 likes, including those who watched the interview when it was broadcast live Thursday morning (during the first few minutes the number of viewers was in the 40s). Forget Wembley: their audience might have struggled to fill Truro City. Rajan is dreaming big, but on the evidence of the debut it might be harder going than he envisaged.

There was a time when journalists, tradesmen that they are, could dream of only a handful of career peaks. You might become an editor or a famous columnist, write a bestseller, get yourself on the telly or make a lucrative sideways move into PR. That was about it.

Barely into his 40s, Amol Rajan has already achieved several of these goals. He edited The Independent at a prodigiously young age. When he was a presenter on the Today programme, nearly six million people heard him grill politicians at breakfast time. Succeeding Jeremy Paxman as host of University Challenge, Rajan has been burnished by proximity to some of the nation’s nerdiest young people.

He was the lovable South London charmer, a state-school boy in a sea of private education, well on his way to national treasure status. According to published figures, he was paid more than £300,000 annually for his BBC work and earned more than £100,000 in outside gigs. A good life, by most measures.

But being a famous journalist is not enough these days. One must become a media empire.

“The BBC, and BBC News, is going to get smaller at an accelerating rate. And I want to go to where the action is,” Rajan has explained (on George Osborne’s podcast).

The internet’s enormous scale has allowed humble hacks to dream of industrial wealth. Hence the Amol Rajan Connection website, a “great digital Narnia” that promises to be a home for Rajan’s YouTube channel, newsletters, events and other content to help his audience navigate a big, scary world. While Rajan has yet to divulge all the details of the content, there are already a number of options to pay, including a “Negroni” tier (£299 a year, which includes a “virtual meet & greet with Amol”) and a “Pina Colada” (£999 for life membership, featuring a “meet & greet at all live events you attend”). Presumably at some stage there will be T-shirts. Thursday’s broadcast was, according to the blurb on YouTube, “brought to you in partnership with” an impressive array of sponsors, including Amazon, NatWest and Waitrose.

To an extent we can blame Gary Lineker for this curious state of affairs. The former England striker’s unlikely reinvention as an audiovisual tycoon with Goalhanger, responsible for the Rest Is… stable of podcasts, has pound signs spinning all over Fleet Street. Then there are Tucker Carlson and Piers Morgan, who have set up their own channels with great success. Carlson has nearly six millions subscribers on YouTube; Morgan is not far behind on 4.5 million. They have proved it is possible to build a large audience while cutting out the pesky networks.

But both men have finely tuned instincts for outrage, not to mention an appetite for confrontation. Carlson was forged in the reactionary fires of Fox News, Morgan in Nineties tabloids. They know that the internet loves rage, have no qualms about encouraging it and have hired smart people to maximise its impact. Rajan’s interview with Southgate – covering the not-unfamiliar territory of the former England manager’s career and concerns about problems facing young men – was perfectly fluent and thoughtful, but on the Today programme he would have been expected to generate multiple headlines.

It will not stop him, or others, from trying their luck. He is not alone in being lured away from his parent institution by the promise of online megastardom. Marina Hyde, the longtime Guardian columnist, recently quit to focus on podcasts, having developed a taste for it alongside Richard Osman on Lineker’s The Rest Is Entertainment. Holly Willoughby, the TV presenter, recently started her own YouTube channel, in which she chunters amiably with other celebrities. She has had disappointing viewing figures, too. Her channel is called Holly Willoughby Together. “Together” and “Connection”. They are positive, hopeful ideas. But positivity and hope do not do well online.

data.title: Healey must not launch another tax raid on banks
data.description:
It has been rare since the financial crash to hear a chancellor single out Britain’s banks for praise. So it was welcome that John Healey on Thursday described them as part of the “jewel in the British economic crown”. Having taken this enlightened stance, however, is he really going to use his Budget to launch yet another tax raid on one of Britain’s most productive sectors?

Reports indicate that this is one of the options the Chancellor is now considering, as he seeks to shore up the public finances. Unions are angry that banks are back to making healthy profits, after the lean years following the financial crisis. They are calling on Mr Healey to increase the surcharge that banks pay on top of ordinary corporation tax.

That might appease Leftists who do not understand why a profitable banking sector is vital to a healthy economy. Banks are one of Britain’s few remaining sources of high-value employment, their lending supports households and businesses, and financial services are a significant export earner for the country.

A tax rise would be hugely damaging not just to the banks, but to the millions of people who hold their shares in pension funds. It is already perverse that banks have to pay a higher rate of corporation tax than other businesses. One only has to look to the disastrous impact of windfall taxes on the North Sea to see what could follow any move to increase the surcharge further.

Business should know by now to take Labour’s warm words with a pinch of salt. In the run-up to the 2024 general election, the party wooed corporate Britain relentlessly. Rachel Reeves called Labour “the natural party of British business”. More than 120 business leaders signed an open letter backing the party, while the Confederation of British Industry welcomed Labour’s manifesto. Their reward has been two of the biggest tax-raising Budgets in history.

Mr Healey may need to find up to £35bn to meet existing spending commitments and boost defence, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. He must know that raising taxes to do so would have dire consequences for economic growth, which only seems to be limping along thanks to strong investment in artificial intelligence.

Too often, Labour politicians view the most successful parts of the economy as morally suspect. Mr Healey claims to understand that they are, in fact, national assets. The Budget is his chance to prove it.

data.title: AstraZeneca dumped by investors over £300bn US merger talks
data.description:
AstraZeneca shares have taken an £18bn hit after investors baulked at reports it was plotting a mega-merger with a US rival.

Shares in Britain’s second-most valuable company slumped on Monday after it emerged that AstraZeneca had held talks about a potential $400bn (£300bn) tie-up with Bristol Myers Squibb.

If completed, the merger would create one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical businesses. The potential deal would also raise fears that AstraZeneca could shift its business to the US in a blow to Britain.

However, analysts said it was a high-risk deal that risked destroying more value than it created. It would be one of the biggest mergers of all time, meaning any missteps could prove hugely costly, and would be likely to draw the attention of competition regulators and politicians.

News of the talks, first reported by the Financial Times, sent AstraZeneca’s shares plunging 9pc on Monday to their lowest level since September 2025.

Markus Manns, a portfolio manager at Union Investment and an ‌AstraZeneca ⁠shareholder, told Reuters: “A combination with Bristol ​does not make strategic or financial sense.

“Many past mega-mergers have destroyed value and there is no apparent need for Astra to do it.”

Jefferies analysts said in a note: “If there is ​one company that doesn’t need financial engineering, it’s AstraZeneca.”

Michael Leuchten, an analyst at Jefferies, said he was “perplexed” by the potential takeover. He said investors backed the company because of its consistent sales growth, not because management “go out and do big deals”.

AstraZeneca is worth around £184bn on the London Stock Exchange, while New York-listed Bristol Myers Squibb has a market value of $133bn.

Bristol Myers Squibb shares surged as much as 3.8pc on Wall Street on Monday.

Analysts said competition concerns would be the biggest hurdle to a deal as both companies have large cancer treatment businesses.

The potential deal could also trigger a political backlash from Donald Trump’s administration, Jefferies warned.

Mr Leuchten added: “AstraZeneca would effectively be a UK-based acquirer of one of America’s large Pharmas, at a time when US policymakers are focused on domestic manufacturing and strategic industries.”

The deal would raise questions about AstraZeneca’s continued links to Britain as Sir Pascal Soriot, its chief executive, pushes ahead with a pivot towards the US.

AstraZeneca upgraded its listing on the New York Stock Exchange last September to let American investors buy its shares directly, while keeping its listing in London.

The move put AstraZeneca’s New York listing on a par with that of London, in what was seen as a blow to the UK’s struggling stock market.

AstraZeneca subsequently struck a $50bn deal with the Trump administration to invest in US manufacturing and transatlantic research facilities.

At the time, Sir Pascal described the drugmaker as a “very American company”.

The business subsequently agreed to sell some medicines at a discount to the US Medicaid programme to avoid being hit with tariffs.

Despite this, Britain’s biggest drugmaker has insisted that it intends to remain headquartered in Cambridge and retain its listing on the London Stock Exchange.

Mr Leuchten said buying Bristol Myers Squibb as a way to shift permanently to the US would be “a fairly drastic way to go about it”.

However, Neil Birrell, the chief investment officer at Premier Miton, an AstraZeneca shareholder, said the likelihood of the pharmaceutical business shifting its shares to the US would increase if the Bristol Myers Squibb deal went ahead.

Mr Birrell added: “There hasn’t been a huge amount that I’ve seen coming out from any of the authorities – whether it be the Government or the London Stock Exchange – of any great substance to try and keep these sort of companies here.”

The Prime Minister said the talks were “a private matter for the companies involved”.

A No 10 spokesman said: “More broadly, the UK life sciences sector is one of our greatest national assets, driving innovation, skilled employment and investment across the country while developing medicines that improve health outcomes and save lives.”

AstraZeneca has around 10,000 staff at five UK sites, including 4,000 at its main facilities in Cambridge and Macclesfield and another 2,000 in London and Luton.

Steve Boden, a regional organiser at GMB Union, said he was seeking urgent assurances from AstraZeneca that jobs would be protected.

“These reports of a merger are causing great concern amongst AstraZeneca’s loyal workers. While no deal has been formally announced, mergers can create pressure to cut costs, so staff are understandably worrying about what this could mean for them.”

The proposed mega-merger will evoke memories of Pfizer’s attempts to take over AstraZeneca a decade ago.

The US company’s acquisition ultimately collapsed after a wave of resistance from the board and politicians alike.

Ed Miliband, then Labour leader, said at the time that Pfizer’s assurances about protecting research and saving jobs were “worthless”.

Bristol Myers Squibb is headquartered in Princeton, New Jersey, and was started in 1858, making it one of the US’s oldest pharmaceutical companies.

data.title: Airlines banned from charging parents to sit next to their children
data.description:
Airlines will be banned from charging parents extra to sit with their children on flights.

The Government has proposed a set of rules requiring airlines to seat children under the age of 14 next to their parents or an accompanying adult free of charge.

According to the Department for Transport, it can cost a parent up to £104 to arrange to sit next to their child on a return journey.

Passengers will also no longer need to pay to tweak the name on their flight booking to correct a mistake.

It is thought ministers will bring in the changes before the start of next year’s summer holidays.

MPs are debating a new set of rules for travel companies as the Civil Aviation (Consumer Protection and Regulatory Reform) Bill makes its way through Parliament.

The proposed law will give ministers powers to draw up a list of passenger rights and a list of duties which both airlines and airports must undertake.

‘Giving people room to breathe’

Andy Burnham said: “Charging parents just to sit with their children is a rip-off, plain and simple. And being hit with a hefty fee for a simple spelling mistake on a booking form isn’t right either.

“People are fed up with these little charges that add up, so I’m putting a stop to them.

“This is what our everyday fixes are all about – giving people room to breathe by tackling the small irritations that catch people out, waste their time and cost them money.”

Rory Boland, the editor of consumer magazine Which? Travel, said: “It’s clearly unfair to force parents and children as young as three to pay an extra fee just to sit together.

“Airlines that have separated families are putting profit ahead of passenger peace of mind.”

Earlier this year, Ryanair adjusted its family seating policy after an investigation was launched into the company charging parents to sit with their children on flights.

The Irish operator previously required parents travelling with children between two and 11 years old to pay to reserve what it referred to as a mandatory family seat. Children were then allocated seats next to or near parents free of charge.

The fee for a mandatory family seat was typically about £8 each way, the UK Competition and Markets Authority found.

At the time, Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair, said its previous policy was “the most progressive and transparent in Europe”.

Heidi Alexander, the Transport Secretary, has also announced a crackdown on bad behaviour by passengers on aircraft, with the Government, airlines and trade unions working on a system to share information about disruptive passengers.

Airlines logged more than 1,000 serious disruptive passenger incidents in 2025, government figures show, including what it described as a mid-air brawl that caused a flight to be diverted.

Using the information-sharing system, airlines could choose to ban persistently disruptive passengers from their aircraft.

“Everyone deserves to travel knowing their flight isn’t going to be disrupted by bad behaviour from a small minority,” Ms Alexander said.

“These common-sense reforms will make flying safer for staff and passengers and protect people from unnecessary charges, whoever they fly with.”

data.title: Putin has ordered ‘General Armageddon’ to smash the bridges of Kyiv. This is why
data.description:
As winter approaches, Vladimir Putin is resorting to the one weapon he has consistently used when his armies fail on the battlefield: terrorising civilians and smashing cities. He has just brought in General Sergei Surovikin – aka “General Armageddon” who flattened the Syrian city of Aleppo, killing thousands of civilians in the process – to do the same to Kyiv.

Putin needs something to change in Ukraine, as the Russian offensive in the Donbas has been in serious trouble for months. Ukrainian forces are pushing back around Pokrovsk and Lyman, while Russian casualties remain extraordinary. President Volodymyr Zelensky has claimed that more than 10,000 Russian soldiers were killed in a single week.

Whether that precise figure is ultimately verified or not, there is no doubt that Putin is paying a staggering price for very limited territorial gains. And now he is running short of men: it is getting difficult to recruit enough volunteer “kontraktniki” contract soldiers to replace the losses.

In theory, Putin could simply launch a mobilisation, which would yield huge numbers of new troops. But the Kremlin knows that another major mobilisation, potentially involving hundreds of thousands of Russians, could be politically explosive. The dictator therefore needs a dramatic change in the military equation before he is forced into a decision that could threaten his grip on power.

His answer is becoming increasingly obvious: if Russia cannot defeat Ukraine’s army, it will try to break the Ukrainian people and nation this winter. This is not a new tactic. Putin supported Bashar al-Assad’s brutal campaign in Syria, where I saw first hand what happened when hospitals, schools and civilian areas became targets for Russian firepower.

The calculation was simple: kill, wound and brutalise enough civilians – make their lives dangerous and horrible enough – and eventually they will demand that their own government ends the war. It failed in Syria. It is likely to fail in Ukraine too.

Kyiv is now under almost relentless attack. There were 18 air raid alerts in the capital on Tuesday alone. Russian missiles and drones are striking deep into the city, damaging civilian infrastructure and even hitting the National Academy of Sciences.

The seven bridges across the Dnipro are obvious targets. Kyiv, like most capital cities, is a major road and rail nexus. If it can be cut in half, that has a paralysing effect on the whole of northern Ukraine: imagine the effect on south eastern England if every bridge in London (including those on the M25) were down.

This is not the behaviour of a man preparing to end his war. It is the behaviour of a dictator preparing his population for a longer one.

The danger is that Putin has identified a vulnerability. Ukraine’s stocks of air-defence munitions are under enormous pressure. High-end interceptor missiles such as the US Patriot are in particularly short supply. Moscow knows this. It is therefore adapting its tactics, moving beyond military targets and increasingly seeking to cripple the infrastructure that allows Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities to function.

This is precisely why the West must understand what Putin is attempting before it is too late. His calculation has always been brutally simple: can Russia outlast its opponent? Putin believes it can.

He has shown an extraordinary willingness to sacrifice Russian soldiers. To the Kremlin, human life is a cheap commodity. Russia has a far larger population than Ukraine and has progressively placed its economy on a war footing. Putin therefore believes that Russia can absorb casualties for longer than Ukraine can stand the punishment and, crucially, for longer than Western governments can maintain public and political support.

That last is the real battle. The question is not simply whether Ukraine can hold Pokrovsk or Lyman. It is whether Britain and Europe have the political stamina to ensure that Ukraine is still standing next year, and the year after that.

I am not convinced that our Government fully understands this. The Prime Minister has explicitly stated that, to him, social security is more important than national security. His priorities are upside down. You cannot deliver social security if you are not secure as a nation.

The West must dramatically increase supplies of air-defence missiles, radars, drones and electronic-warfare systems. But we should also be prepared to consider measures that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago.

If Russia deliberately targets civilian infrastructure on an industrial scale, Nato must consider how its overwhelming air power could be used to protect Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure without directly entering the war. That does not necessarily mean declaring a traditional no-fly zone tomorrow. It means seriously examining whether Nato aircraft could help defend defined areas or critical infrastructure in extremis, particularly where the alternative is allowing Russian missiles and drones to slaughter civilians with impunity.

The Geneva Conventions are clear: the proper laws of war – not overblown human rights rules, but the regular laws of war – forbid deliberate targeting of civilians without any military purpose. Just when Ukraine appears to be gaining momentum on the battlefield, Putin is attempting to move the war on to ground where he believes Russia has the advantage: a test of civilian endurance.

We must not let him.

Ukraine’s army is fighting back in the Donbas. Its soldiers are inflicting enormous losses on the Russian military. This is precisely the moment when the West should be leaning forward, not stepping back. Putin understands strength, but understands weakness even better.

If we allow him to discover that bombing Kyiv works, he will do more of it. If, instead, Britain and Europe demonstrate that Ukraine’s cities will be defended, its people will be supported and its army will be supplied for as long as necessary, Putin may finally understand the one thing he has so far refused to accept: Russia cannot bomb and meat-grind its way to victory.

data.title: Minister rejects boost to gas storage despite threat of shortages
data.description:
A minister has rejected calls to invest in Britain’s largest gas storage facility despite growing fears of winter fuel shortages.

Luke Pollard, the defence minister, said that the emergency gas storage facility, known as Rough, “is not something that the Government is choosing to invest in”.

Rough, which is located in the North Sea and operated by British Gas owner Centrica, represents about half of Britain’s gas storage capacity.

Bosses at Centrica have warned the facility could close by April 2027 unless the site receives government support, leaving a major gap in the nation’s energy reserves.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Mr Pollard said: “Centrica are a big company with deep pockets. They can choose their investments that they want to make.”

He added: “This is a very clear commercial decision for the company.

“The steps that we’re taking as a Government are to come off the fossil fuel roller-coaster with more investment in renewables.”

He made the comments after Chris O’Shea, Centrica’s chief executive, warned that the loss-making facility was needed to safeguard national security.

Centrica has been in talks with ministers for a cap-and-floor mechanism to help fund a £2bn injection into the gas facility.

The FTSE 100 company would supply the investment up front, but the scheme would effectively mean guaranteed funding underwritten by a levy on household energy bills.

Mr O’Shea said: “The future of Rough is too important to the UK to be dismissed as simply a ‘commercial decision’.

“The UK’s energy security cannot be taken for granted, and Rough is an opportunity to strengthen our national security and resilience, safeguard existing jobs, create new ones and drive investment and growth in the UK – delivering on the Government’s own ambition to reindustrialise Britain.”

He said the FTSE 100 company was not asking taxpayers to fund the investment, but was instead “asking for the Government to apply its existing cap-and-floor regulatory framework to unlock it”.

Mr O’Shea added: “We are ready to invest £2bn of our own money in critical national infrastructure. Government should not allow this opportunity to be lost.”

The Government has yet to make a formal decision on the future of Rough and a spokesman declined to comment.

The UK, along with other European countries, is going into winter with some of the lowest levels of gas storage in years.

Supplies from the Middle East remain disrupted because of the Iran war and damage to liquefied natural gas infrastructure across the Gulf.

The wholesale price of European gas rose to its highest level in four years on Tuesday at nearly €87 per megawatt hour after increasing for six consecutive days.

Gas prices were around €32 per megawatt hour before the Iran war started.

Tancrede Fulop, an analyst at Morningstar, said higher gas prices were being driven by “unusually low storage levels for this time of year as the heating season begins”.

He added: “Supply disruptions in the Gulf have also intensified competition with Asian buyers for US LNG.”

A report released last week by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas found that the UK’s gas storage facilities could be completely depleted by spring if a cold snap sweeps across the country.

Warnings about low energy reserves come as pressure grows on Andy Burnham to approve the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas and oil fields.

However, objections from environmental groups have meant the Government has repeatedly delayed the decision.

Separately, shares in BP climbed to a six-month high on Tuesday after the energy giant revealed it had been able to cut its debt pile by a third thanks to soaring oil and gas prices.

The FTSE 100 business said its net debt would fall to below $14.5bn (£10.9bn) in the third quarter, down from $22.3bn.

data.title: Britain’s gas pipelines are in Putin’s crosshairs
data.description:
Sign up here for more exclusive insight from Ambrose Evans-Pritchard in our Economic Intelligence newsletter, delivered direct to your inbox every Tuesday.

In the last days of September, a Russian-controlled tanker loitered for 40 hours over critical North Sea pipelines supplying the St Fergus Gas Terminal, responsible for 25-50pc of the UK’s total gas consumption.

Three days later, a Chinese-flagged tanker – but really part of Russia’s shadow fleet, according to Ukrainian intelligence – followed up at the same spot east of Shetland.

“Both behaved identically, drifting for six to 24 hours, steaming a few miles back, then drifting again,” said Windward Maritime Intelligence.

“The second vessel stopped on the edge of the Flags pipeline corridor, then spent 11 hours within one nautical mile of the Alwyn-Frigg pipeline,” it said.

Days earlier, two Russian tugs had loitered over Danish electricity and data cables in the Kattegat corridor. One was towing an excavator barge capable of working the seabed. Neither had any visible commercial activity.

The last few weeks have seen an alarming increase in latent undersea warfare by Russia and China, perhaps in collusion, from Canada’s Grand Banks, to Guam, Japan and the Luzon Strait in the Far East.

But what worries me right now is the security of the UK’s gas supply, both from its own offshore fields and from Norway. This is our immediate Achilles heel.

“We’re very vulnerable. Russians have learned that attacks on gas infrastructure have more impact than anything else,” said Prof Kevin Rowlands, from the Royal United Services Institute.

“If one of these pipelines is attacked, you’re looking at weeks and months, not days, and if there are multiple breaks it’s even worse. You could put explosive devices on undersea drones and explode them,” he said.

Prof Rowlands, who used to head the Royal Navy Strategic Studies Centre, added: “No arm of the British state has the capability to repair the pipelines. It is up to private commercial companies, and there is a lot of confusion over who is responsible.”

He said the national debate has been overly focused on the threat to data cables and is underplaying what may now be the greater danger.

“Data cables are easier to attack because you can drag an anchor over them, but there are more than 60 so there is greater redundancy. It may cause temporary damage, but there are ways to reroute the data traffic,” he said.

Sir David Omand, the former director of GCHQ, said the UK is in the Kremlin’s “crosshairs” because of its role in the Ukraine war. “We really must expect the Russians to pick on us,” he told a parliamentary inquiry on subsea warfare.

The joint committee’s report last year was a sobering indictment of past complacency. “We were disturbed about the level of scepticism we encountered in some parts of industry and government about the value of preparing for more extensive co-ordinated attacks,” it said.

“Some suggested we should focus on fishing accidents or low-level hybrid sabotage. We are not persuaded that this is a good basis for mitigating catastrophic risk.”

Prof Rowlands said Russia’s latest mischief off the Shetlands is probably just another probing action to test our response. “A blatant attack has not been their modus so far. They like deniability,” he said.

But we do know that Vladimir Putin is apt to escalate suddenly. He is an opportunistic aggressor and acts only when the stars are aligned for his purposes. He waited for two critical developments before launching his European gas squeeze in mid-2021, the precursor to the invasion of Ukraine eight months later.

The first was the global gas shortage coming out of Covid. The second was Joe Biden’s fateful deal with Angela Merkel, the former German chancellor, to waive US sanctions on Russia’s Nord Stream pipeline, which Putin took to be permission to try his luck.

We now have an equally disturbing confluence of events. Wholesale gas prices in Europe have tripled to €85 per megawatt-hour since Donald Trump set fire to the Middle East in February. Today it is six times the average level of the pre-Covid years. It could double again.

The UK has just seven days’ supply on its own territory. The Rough storage site is still largely empty because of a dispute with Centrica about who pays the cost.

This country has subcontracted its gas storage to the Continent, but Europe’s own sites were not sufficiently replenished during the summer because buyers were holding out for lower prices, thinking the Iran war would soon be over.

EU-wide storage is at the lowest seasonal level in 15 years. Germany and the Netherlands are at the lowest ever recorded.

Trump has made matters more dangerous with the cynical charade of his diesel deal with Putin. Russia cannot add net supply to the fungible world market in any plausible time frame. S&P Global Energy says half of Russia’s refining capacity is out of action because of Ukrainian drone strikes, which have been hitting the catalytic crackers that take at least six months to repair.

Putin is having to import fuel from India and Kazakhstan. He may even be importing diesel from Iran via rail links and the Caspian, which implies that any “Russian” diesel that reaches the US – if any does – may in fact be Iranian. Need one add credible reports that the Kremlin is helping Iran to kill American servicemen with targeting intelligence?

The deal nevertheless matters because it does significant political damage. Trump has comprehensively undermined the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act – passed by 86 to 11 in the Senate – which he himself signed into law four weeks ago.

At the same time we learn that the Trump family, in all its nepotistic shamelessness, is actively negotiating with the Kremlin to carve up the global assets of the Russian oil company Lukoil. It is discussing some sort of stake in a Nord Stream revival. A cynic might conclude that Putin has succeeded in recruiting Trump – for a fee – as his full accomplice.

Britain is now in a dangerous predicament. Anybody who still thinks Trump would defend us against a Russian threat of nuclear escalation needs their head examined. We fall back on a European and Canadian Nato, but our nuclear weapons are inadequate, with no tactical or mid-range rungs on the ladder. We should not be surprised if the Kremlin starts to test this.

Successive British governments have been negligent. We should have started rearming when Putin attacked Georgia in 2008, changing the borders in Europe by force for the first time since the Second World War. We should have lifted defence spending to 3pc of GDP after he seized Crimea and much of the Donbas in 2014.

We should put our economy on a war footing of 4pc of GDP after he tried to extinguish Ukraine altogether in 2022, and we should have gone to 5pc as soon as Trump threatened Canada, Greenland, and (implicitly) the Falklands.

Instead we frittered away £100bn on runaway benefits for able-bodied youth and on gas subsidies that went mostly to the overheated middle classes, who have since made pitiful efforts to prepare for the next shock that is now hitting us.

As a British citizen and taxpayer, I am vexed.

data.title: Blocking Jackdaw and Rosebank ‘would cost Britain £11bn’
data.description:
Britain will miss out on thousands of jobs and almost £11bn in tax if ministers block the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields, researchers have claimed.

A study commissioned by Adura, the energy company behind the two projects, concluded that the Treasury would miss out on £10.9bn of revenue by 2049-50 if the Government did not approve drilling.

Similarly, analysts said the North Sea energy schemes could create more than 3,000 extra jobs – a benefit that local economies would miss out on should the projects be rejected.

The research looked at the extra jobs and taxes that Adura might generate if the two schemes go ahead, compared with what the company might produce if their plans are rejected.

The Government is considering whether Rosebank and Jackdaw, which were approved by the previous Conservative administration, should be given the go-ahead.

Labour promised a ban on new drilling in the North Sea in its 2024 election manifesto, but Rosebank and Jackdaw have fallen into a politically challenging grey area. While Rosebank and Jackdaw were technically already approved, legal wrangling has forced developers to go back to the Government to sign off on them a second time.

Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has pledged to take a “pragmatic” approach to the North Sea and is expected to approve Jackdaw, a gas field located 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

However, he was accused of delaying the decision to avoid political embarrassment before last week’s Holborn and St Pancras by-election, which Labour won with the Green Party in second place.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the Energy Secretary, said in the Commons on Tuesday that her department was “making decisions at pace”. She told MPs: “Any decision I make will be compatible with our climate commitments.”

Environmental campaigners and Labour backbenchers argue that permitting more fossil fuel projects would undermine UK climate targets, increase fossil fuel dependency and bring few economic benefits.

But Prof John Underhill, the director for energy transition at the University of Aberdeen, said “deliberately accelerating the decline” of North Sea oil “would be a catastrophic error”.

Writing in The Telegraph, he said: “Every additional barrel produced from the North Sea is one Britain and our European neighbours do not have to source from Russia, the Middle East, the United States or elsewhere in an increasingly uncertain world.

“Energy security is national security, both for Britain and our European allies.”

The analysis by Public First for Adura finds that the two schemes would help Adura generate £35bn for the UK economy between 2026 and 2035, compared with £24.5bn if their oil and gas were “left in the ground”.

It said: “Under the ‘oil left in the ground’ scenario, cumulative tax revenues are lower by £2.6bn between 2026-27 and 2035-36, and by £10.9bn by 2049-50.”

Rosebank is the UK’s largest undeveloped oil field. It lies in Atlantic waters about 60 miles west of the Shetland under about 3,000ft of sea and a similar depth of rock. It holds an estimated 500 million barrels of oil.

Neil McCulloch, the chief executive of Adura, said: “Failure to approve Rosebank and other planned developments would mean billions of pounds less economic value for the UK and thousands fewer jobs supported every year.”

Katherine May, the head of Oxfam Scotland, said: “It’s hardly surprising that a report commissioned by an oil company concludes that more drilling is a good idea.

“Asking it to assess Jackdaw and Rosebank is like asking a seagull whether chips should be left unguarded.”

How the North Sea can help Britain avoid another fuel crisis

By John Underhill

Twenty-six years ago, Britain ground to a halt as protests at oil refineries and fuel distribution depots became a national crisis.

Petrol stations ran dry, supermarkets struggled to keep shelves stocked, hospitals cancelled appointments, businesses warned they were days from shutting down and the roads fell eerily silent.

It was a dramatic demonstration of something we usually take for granted, which is that modern economies cannot function without fuel.

Today, as Britain becomes increasingly dependent on imported diesel, we should remember that lesson.

In the early 2000s, the UK produced more than enough diesel to meet its own needs. Since then, that resilience, along with much of our refining capacity, has been steadily dismantled.

The closure of Grangemouth and Lindsey last year accelerated that decline, and today more than half of the diesel Britain needs must now come from overseas.

That matters because, despite the drive towards electrification, the country still runs on hydrocarbons. Around 15 million cars and heavy goods vehicles use diesel, including the lorries that move food and goods around the country. Emergency and military vehicles depend on it too, while diesel generators provide back-up power for critical infrastructure.

For years, our growing dependence on imports attracted little attention because global supplies were plentiful and prices relatively low. The past five years have exposed the weakness in that assumption.

Russia was once a major source of diesel for Britain and Europe, but those supplies disappeared after the invasion of Ukraine. Turmoil in the Middle East has since provided another reminder of how quickly apparently secure supplies can become vulnerable, leaving Britain increasingly reliant on diesel shipped across the Atlantic.

If America were to restrict diesel exports in response to its own domestic pressures, as has been threatened, the consequences for Britain and Europe could be profound.

We know what happens when fuel stops moving because we saw it in September 2000. But there is an important difference between then and now.

Back then, we had the fuel. The problem was moving it out of refineries and distribution terminals. Today, an increasing proportion of the fuel that Britain depends on is not produced here at all.

That makes the debate about our remaining domestic energy resources all the more important.

Opponents of developments such as Rosebank argue that North Sea oil does little for British energy security because much of it will be exported. That fundamentally misunderstands how our energy system works.

Britain is part of a deeply integrated European energy market in which crude oil and refined products move between countries according to the capabilities of refineries and the needs of consumers.

North Sea crude exported to a refinery in the Netherlands or Belgium does not cease to contribute to our energy security when it leaves UK waters. It enters a European refining system that produces the diesel, petrol and aviation fuel consumed across the continent, including products imported back into Britain.

Every additional barrel produced from the North Sea is one Britain and our European neighbours do not have to source from Russia, the Middle East, the US or elsewhere in an increasingly uncertain world. Energy security is national security, both for Britain and our European allies.

The case for domestic production goes further. It protects highly skilled jobs, supports the supply-chain companies we will need to deliver the energy transition and generates billions in tax revenues that can help ease the burden of fuel duty and household energy bills. Producing more at home also means importing less, improving our balance of payments.

That is why oil projects such as Rosebank are of crucial importance. Their contribution to energy security should not be judged on whether every barrel is landed, refined and consumed within the UK. Energy markets simply do not work that way.

Ministers should see production and refining as two parts of the same strategic challenge: supporting investment in North Sea resources, protecting the refining capacity we still possess and recognising Britain’s role as a major energy producer within the wider European system.

None of this means abandoning the energy transition. It means recognising that the transition must be secure as well as orderly.

Britain and Europe will continue to consume substantial quantities of oil while that transition takes place. The question is whether more of it should come from resources we control, supporting our economy and our allies, or from increasingly uncertain suppliers overseas.

The fuel blockades of 2000 showed how quickly a country could seize up when energy supply chains are interrupted. A quarter of a century later, with fewer British refineries and a more dangerous geopolitical environment, deliberately accelerating the decline of one of Europe’s major sources of oil – the UK North Sea – would be a catastrophic error for Britain and Europe.

Prof John Underhill is director for energy transition at the University of Aberdeen

data.title: US inflation jumps ahead of crunch midterm elections
data.description:
US inflation rose more than expected last month as diesel prices hit record highs just weeks before key mid-term elections to decide who controls Congress.

The consumer prices index rose from 3.4pc in August to 3.7pc in September, the US Department of Labor said, outstripping estimates of a jump to 3.6pc.

More than half of the increase in inflation last month was as a result of surging fuel prices, which climbed by 9.1pc during September.

The higher-than-expected figure sent the cost of US government borrowing surging on Wednesday as traders ramped up bets on the Federal Reserve (Fed) raising interest rates to temper price rises.

The data were published after the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that the global diesel crisis will drag on into next year despite Donald Trump’s claims to have unlocked crucial extra supplies.

The Paris-based organisation said diesel supplies “remained under significant strain” as exports from Russia and the Middle East were disrupted by conflict.

Diesel shortages are expected to continue well into next year, even as record prices are forecast to cause a decline in demand.

In its monthly oil market report, the IEA said: “Despite lower demand, oil market balances are forecast to remain in deficit through the end of the year, with constrained middle distillate supplies likely to persist well into 2027.”

Middle distillate refers to products such as diesel and jet fuel that are created during the refining process.

The IEA’s warning and the jump in inflation are a setback to Mr Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices for motorists before the US midterm elections on Nov 3.

The elections will decide whether the Republicans or Democrats control Congress.

The G7 announced the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel stockpiles earlier this month after pressure from the US president.

Mr Trump had threatened to impose an export ban on diesel as shortages pushed up the price of gasoline in the US to a record above $6.50 a gallon.

He also lifted sanctions on Russian diesel during the weekend in an effort to boost supplies, a move that drew criticism from the international community and members of his own Republican Party.

Giorgia Meloni, the Italian prime minister, described Mr Trump’s agreement on Russian diesel as a “very risky” decision.

She warned on Wednesday that the agreement could send “contradictory” signals at a time when Western countries, including the US, have been seeking to pressure Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine, which has raged since Russia’s invasion in 2022.

The US president has blamed Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries for the increase in diesel prices.

While this has stretched global supplies, analysts say that Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and Mr Trump’s attack on Iran have also contributed to spiralling energy costs.

On Wall Street, the S&P 500 slipped 0.4pc after the latest inflation figures and was on track for a fifth loss in the six days since setting its record high.

Stocks were under pressure from rising borrowing costs, as expectations of higher US interest rates pushed the two-year US Treasury bond yield from 4.79pc to as high as 4.95pc.

Traders are betting that there is around a 47pc chance that the Fed will raise rates to combat rising inflation, compared to odds of 23pc on Tuesday.

Inflation pressures show little sign of easing. The IEA said global oil stocks declined in September after 113 million barrels were drawn down from inventories.

Global diesel exports fell by 700,000 barrels per day in September compared to the same month last year.

The Paris-based organisation said continued disruptions to Middle East exports, compounded by lower supply from Russia and some Asian countries, had cut global diesel availability. This was “putting diesel markets under extreme pressure”.

Diesel remains around £2 a litre at the pumps in the UK, according to RAC, having hit a record high last month.

John Healey, the Chancellor, is under pressure to scrap a planned 5p increase in fuel duty when he delivers his first Budget on Oct 28.

The IEA said high prices were taking their toll on global oil demand, which is expected to drop by 2.5 million barrels per day in the final three months of the year.

Oil was trading at around $106 a barrel on Wednesday, up from around $70 before the start of the Iran war.

Prices showed no sign of easing after a series of strikes on Saudi airports by Houthi rebels. The headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco was also hit during a missile attack on Wednesday.

data.title: Hollywood’s new mogul races to escape an $80bn debt trap
data.description:
“It was not easy to get here,” David Ellison told employees after closing Paramount’s $110bn (£82bn) mega-merger with Warner Bros last week. “At times, it was downright ugly.”

Even Ellison’s most ardent critics will acknowledge that he has pulled off a coup. In a few short years, the 43-year-old has built a media empire in the face of fierce political opposition to emerge as Hollywood’s newest mogul.

Yet troubles at his newly merged company – now rebranded as Skydance – are only just beginning. Despite the backing of his billionaire father Larry Ellison and three Gulf states, David Ellison’s deal was funded primarily through eye-watering sums of debt. Now he must prove that the numbers can add up.

“While David Ellison laid out his company’s priorities, focusing on storytelling, trust, technology and market leadership, he omitted the elephant in the room, which is the necessary cost-cutting that has to happen to deal with the company’s deep debt and satisfy investors,” says Mike Proulx, an analyst at Forrester.

Skydance has a net debt of roughly $80bn, or around seven times its profits. That is almost three times higher than the 2.5x level normally associated with the industry, according to Enders Analysis.

At $5.8bn, the annual cost of servicing this debt will be significant. The question for Ellison is: how does he plan to escape this debt trap?

Skydance brings together two of Hollywood’s biggest studios and their extensive back catalogues of film and TV shows, ranging from the Harry Potter franchise to Game of Thrones and SpongeBob SquarePants, as well as the HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services and the CNN and CBS news networks.

It is an enviable array of intellectual property that gives Skydance the scale to rival both Disney and Netflix.

Yet analysts and rating agencies are raising eyebrows at the financial gymnastics required to combine the two behemoths. Both already carried significant debt from their own formative mergers.

Paramount raised $52bn of debt in just a week as it scrambled to close the deal, which is the largest leveraged buyout in history.

The timing could hardly have been worse, coming amid a wider bond sell-off that has driven up borrowing costs across the market.

Skydance’s finances will be further constrained by legal obligations requiring it to release at least 30 films in cinemas in the US each year and increase US production spend by $1.5bn across five years.

“We have a business plan,” Ynon Kreiz said this week. He is the no-nonsense former boss of toymaker Mattel who has been named co-chief executive of Skydance.

“There’s a complete financial envelope to how we’re going to run the business, and content is a spend, but you can also see it as an investment because it’s also going to drive growth.”

Streaming price rises?

Skydance executives are keen to emphasise the potential for cash generation from a company with revenues of around $70bn. They are aiming to quickly cut the borrowing pile, bringing leverage down to below three times profits by 2029.

The group’s traditional – or “linear” – channels such as CBS, MTV and Nickelodeon, as well as Channel 5 in the UK, remain its most profitable assets. Yet linear is also a business in decline, meaning this will be a dwindling pool of cash to rely on in future.

In streaming, Ellison has confirmed plans to merge HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single service, creating a major new challenger to Netflix.

Around four million UK homes now have access to a Paramount+ subscription, making it the fourth most popular streaming service, though it remains well behind Netflix, Amazon Prime and Disney.

HBO Max, which only launched in the UK in March, was not included in the latest industry figures, but is hoping to scoop up more subscribers ahead of the launch of its new Harry Potter series on Christmas Day.

Given its extensive entertainment catalogue, Skydance could also seek to generate cash by licencing out films and TV shows to other players such as Netflix.

Yet that puts it at risk of giving away its best intellectual property to rivals and undermining the value of its own streaming platforms.

Either way, analysts warn that households will likely end up paying more. “It’s hard to imagine that streaming price hikes aren’t in Skydance’s future,” says Proulx.

Swinging the axe

Ultimately, though, the debt-fuelled takeover will rely heavily on cost-cutting. Ellison has already said he is eyeing savings of $6bn and industry observers describe new boss Kreiz, who previously ran production giant Endemol, as “unsentimental”.

Gerry Cardinale, head of RedBird Capital, the US investment firm that backed the deal, has sought to play down fears of redundancies, pointing to “synergies” in areas including technology and marketing.

Yet job losses are undeniable. Ellison and Kreiz acknowledged this in a memo to staff this week, which warned that “integrating two companies will bring change, including difficult decisions that affect our workforce”.

It is unclear how these cuts will affect the UK, where Skydance owns Channel 5. Lisa Nandy, the Culture Secretary, cleared the deal only after Ellison made a number of commitments, including making more British TV and safeguarding Channel 5’s news and kids’ output.

But in a sign of how Ellison could squeeze Channel 5, newly filed accounts for the British broadcaster this week showed it paid a record £215m dividend to Paramount last year, even as its profits tumbled.

Analysts say office property will be a key target for savings, but there are also fears for the 4,000 Warner Bros employees in the UK.

The deal will also raise further questions about the future of TNT Sports, Warner Bros Discovery’s broadcasting joint venture with BT. Warner Bros had been gearing up to buy out BT’s 50pc stake before the takeover saga, but that prospect is less certain now that it has combined with Paramount’s own sports assets.

Paramount poached the UK rights to show Champions League matches from TNT last year, while it splashed out $7.7bn to secure exclusive rights to the Ultimate Fighting Championship in the US.

Mike Darcey, former chief operating officer at Sky, suggests Skydance could seek to slim down its sprawling array of sports rights as part of its cost-cutting drive. In particular, he highlights the potential £300m saving from dropping its Premier League fixtures.

“If it was the BT team, or even the TNT team, I suspect they would not make this choice,” Darcey says. “But that’s precisely why Ellison has brought in someone like Ynon, because he does not have the history, the internal and external relationships, and can make the tough and unsentimental choices.”

Ellison family’s reputation on the line

Regardless of where the axe falls, there are question marks over how feasible downsizing on this scale really is.

Even after its $6bn of savings, Skydance will need to reduce debt by $26bn – or about $9bn a year – to meet its deleveraging target.

“There’s a hell of a lot built into management synergies required to get leverage down to a level that makes sense,” says Gordon Shannon, partner at TwentyFour Asset Management.

“It means that business just won’t have as much flexibility as its competitors.”

After the deal closed this week, credit ratings agency Fitch downgraded Skydance to BB, putting its bonds in the “junk” category.

Fitch said the downgrade reflected “significant execution and integration risks” and “uncertainty about the company’s ability to achieve its stated synergies, which are material to its deleveraging target”.

Investors may be reassured by the significant equity backing, including the $24bn pumped in by the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi.

Sir Tony Blair has been appointed as an adviser to the Skydance board, raising the prospect that he will serve as a proxy for these Gulf shareholders given his think tank carries out a significant amount of work in the region.

Larry Ellison, meanwhile, agreed to personally backstop $40bn of the equity financing.

Ellison briefly became the world’s richest man last year as his software firm Oracle rode the AI boom. Now, however, questions are growing over whether the 82-year-old, who took on around $130bn in debt to fuel his expansion in data centres, has overstretched himself. Oracle shares are down around 30pc so far this year.

Perhaps in acknowledgement, the company has reportedly explored finding a syndicate of new equity investors to share the load, with Elon Musk among the names discussed.

Such a move would help to ease concerns about the Hollywood giant’s precarious position on top of a mountain of debt.

Ultimately, though, it is the Ellison family that has staked its reputation – and vast amounts of money – on a mammoth deal to reshape Tinseltown. It will be on them to prove the numbers stack up and the deal can work.

data.title: Netflix to cut 1,000 jobs in its biggest ever cull
data.description:
Netflix is to cut up to 1,000 jobs worldwide in the streaming giant’s biggest ever round of cost-cutting.

The US company is preparing to axe around 6pc of its global workforce as it grapples with slowing growth in the crowded streaming market.

The cuts will be focused on Netflix’s product, technology, legal and human resources teams. It is unclear how many job losses will fall in the UK, where the company employs more than 600 people.

Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos, co-chief executives of Netflix, told staff on Wednesday: “Our mission – to entertain the world – is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources.”

It marks Netflix’s biggest ever redundancy round and the first major cost-cutting exercise since 2022, when it laid off around 450 employees in the wake of its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than a decade.

Netflix has emerged as a clear winner in the streaming wars and generated UK revenues of £2bn from its 18 million subscribers last year, eclipsing ITV for the first time.

But it is once again contending with slowing growth as subscriber numbers begin to plateau. The company is under fierce pressure from demanding investors and its share price has slumped by more than 40pc over the last year.

Bosses have cracked down on password-sharing and introduced cheaper, advertising-supported tiers to help maintain revenue growth.

Subscribers have also been subjected to repeated price rises, with the price of a premium package now topping £20.

Netflix is also expanding into new formats in an effort to keep viewers engaged. It is increasingly turning to live TV to drive both new subscriptions and advertising revenues.

Despite previous insistence that it would not move into live sports, the streaming giant has pushed ever further into this area. Netflix this week secured the rights to broadcast the 2030 World Cup in Spain.

Mr Peters and Mr Sarandos insisted that Netflix would continue to invest “aggressively” and it is understood that spending on programming will not be affected by the cuts.

But the bosses acknowledged that the company had to make “focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees and investors”.

The cuts come as Netflix also contends with the creation of a major new rival following the $110bn merger of Paramount and Warner Bros.

David Ellison, who leads the newly renamed Skydance, has confirmed plans to combine the two companies’ streaming services – Paramount+ and HBO Max – into a single platform.

Fierce competition and rising production costs have also prompted job cuts at Disney and Sky owner Comcast as media groups seek to curb costs.

The Netflix cuts, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, come a week before the company’s quarterly results, with bosses insisting it is on track to meet its forecasts for the full year.
